speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTINGS
speechtext:
I should like to substitute for the motion that is on the order paper the following:
That on and after Wednesday, July 12, until the end of the session, the house shall not .be adjourned on Wednesday at six o'clock, notwithstanding anything in standing order No. 6.
I may say that the motion as it appears on the order paper would preclude us from carrying on the understanding we had about Wednesday afternoons and the motion as it is now put will continue the same procedure on Wednesday afternoons as we have been following; that is to say, that members of the war committee would be free to attend meetings of that committee on Wednesday and not be expected to be in the house.

subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTINGS
speechtext: Why pick on the 12th of July?

speakeroldname: Mr. GORDON GRAYDON (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTINGS
speechtext: In view of the situation which has now arisen with respect to the change in sitting hours, I would ask the Prime Minister if the government would not permit some slight modification of the previous arrangement in regard to Wednesdays, so that the orders of the day may be called. If that were done, with the understanding that as usual there will be no divisions that day, perhaps that would be satisfactory as far as we are concerned.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTINGS
speechtext: That means we would have questions and so on?

subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTINGS
speechtext:
Yes. Why not? That is what you started out to do.
LMr. Shaw.]

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTINGS
speechtext: I believe hon. members have found it a little more expeditious to proceed at once on Wednesdays with the business; to have one day when the house is not liable to be held up by questions or motions. I would say to my hon. friends that it would be embarrassing to members of the government if they were not in the house in the event of certain motions being moved on Wednesday afternoons. It will be necessary for the members of the war committee to continue to meet on Wednesday afternoons as they have met in the past.

subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTINGS
speechtext:
I am sure there is no desire to embarrass the government or the war committee of the cabinet; I want the Prime Minister to understand that at the very outset of any remarks I have to make. The arrangement entered into early in the session, on the Prime Minister's own initiative, under which the house did not sit on Wednesday, did not work out as he had anticipated. So far as I am concerned, and I think so far as most of the private members of this house are concerned it was a day wasted.' The Prime Minister then permitted the business to be dealt with on Wednesday afternoons, and that has continued up to the present time. Now, near the end of the session, he brings in a very proper motion that the order of business on Wednesday shall be the same as on other days. That is the motion on the order paper, but for some reason, which he suggests as being interference with the cabinet or the war committee, he wants to take away from private members on Wednesdays one of the few privileges remaining to them. I do protest against that limitation, and others I could mention. This notice of motion on the order paper is the proper notice that should be given if we are to cariy on the business of the house in a proper way. Evidently the government have had a change of heart and a change of mind, but I do not believe they are justified in attempting to take away from private members at this late stage of the session, one of their few remaining privileges.
I protest against it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTINGS
speechtext:
There has been no change of heart or of mind on the part of the government. As a matter of fact if I had not intervened yesterday, at the time I spoke of the house sitting Wednesday evenings, I believe the motion would have been put at that time and what I am now suggesting would have been adopted. I asked that a motion be placed upon the order paper providing that the house would resume its sittings on Wednesday evenings. I did not

Mobilization Act
see the motion until I was coming into the house. I then sent for the Clerk, and pointed out to him that the motion appearing on the order paper would make it necessary for members of the war committee to be in the house Wednesday afternoons; that I felt it imperative that we should have Wednesday afternoons for the meetings of the war committee; I asked the Clerk to give me a substitute motion which would permit the proceedings on Wednesday afternoons being carried on as they have been since hon. gentlemen opposite were kind enough to make what they said was a constructive suggestion, that by omitting questions on the orders of the day we would save a great deal of time. I thanked my 'hon. friends for the suggestion at the time; I should like to continue to thank them for making it possible to have the house carry on as they originally suggested. It is in every way preferable that we should save time which, as hon. members know, is liable to be taken up with questions and unexpected matters which otherwise would come up on Wednesday afternoon. If hon. members are desirous of having the business of the house drag on; if that is their real wish, for my part I do not mind if I stay here until the month of December. I am prepared to remain in this house and follow its proceedings to the end, but I do think everyone is anxious to expedite business, and that has been the sole motive in presenting these motions.

subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTINGS
speechtext: May I ask that a definite understanding be arrived at in regard to divisions on Wednesdays?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTINGS
speechtext: There are to be none.	'

subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTINGS
speechtext: There are to be no divisions? Are we to understand that this will also cover votes in committee? A couple of Wednesdays ago an incident arose which made me wonder whether that general understanding was supposed to cover votes in committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTINGS
speechtext: My understanding was that any contentious question would be postponed, that we would not have a division that day. It had better be the definite understanding in regard to both divisions and votes in committee. It is just a matter of dropping the particular item for the time being, and taking it up at a subsequent time.

subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTINGS
speechtext: But that does not cover the matter of committees.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTINGS
speechtext: Yes. in regard to both.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTINGS
speechtext: During the debate on the aeronautics bill or the transport bill a couple of weeks ago, if my memory serves me correctly, the question of an appeal from the ruling of the Chair came up, and in my temporary absence from the house the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) said he was quite sure I would support his contention that there could not be a division in the house while this arrangement was in effect, which of course placed us in an awkward position. I think there should be some clarification in that regard, because it might bring about an embarrassing situation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: WEDNESDAY SITTINGS
speechtext: I think we might understand that if hon. members object to any matters being discussed further at that stage, that matter might be dropped for the time being and something else taken up.

speechtext: Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed from Monday, July 10, consideration of the motion of Hon. J. L. Hsley (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Rowe.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during the course of my remarks last night I indicated my intention to make reference to certain observations made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank). I do that, not because that hon. member happens to be involved, but because of the necessity for stating more clearly certain things which altogether too frequently are represented in an entirely improper light.
I refer to page 4684 of Hansard, where the hon. member said:
I entirely disagree with the government on their man-power policy and am not afraid to say so, but I must say at the same time that every party in the house made the same mistake in 1940.
So far as the Social Credit party is concerned, that statement is not correct. I shall endeavour to show the house in a moment or two, as we have shown before, what our stand was at that time. Again the hon. member said, as reported on the same page:
The fact of the matter is that none of us was prepared to face the public and say that we would put conscription into force from the drop of the hat, although we represented the people of Canada.

Again, so far as the Social Credit party is concerned, that statement is not correct. Third, and finally, he said:
None of the parties had courage to face the public and say that it would put conscription *into force at the very outset, as the United States and Great Britain did.
The Social Credit party is the one party which did have the courage, and to that extent the hon. member's statement is not correct.
Let me go back to 1936, when members of the Social Credit party first entered the House of Commons. I have referred to this statement before. The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), house leader of this party, referring to the general prospects and the existing dangers of that day, said:
The increase of armaments that is in prospect is a most disappointing development to all who want to see the reign of law established in international affairs and an end put to war. But where the responsibility lies is quite clear. No matter bow peace-loving a nation may ibe it has to consider the conditions which exist in the world to-day and act accordingly. Britain has been exceedingly anxious to avoid adding to their armament burdens but in its present situation has no alternative. Nor can Canada be content with merely expressing the desire for peace.
The hon. member for Lethbridge went on at that time and indicated that this group would support such steps on Canada's part as would render her powerful enough in all respects to plan an effective part in any world crisis with which the League of Nations might be called upon to deal.
Then, he made other statements. I could take Hansard from 1936, right up to the present time, and prove conclusively to the house that the Social Credit party not only took the correct stand at the beginning, but is the only party in the house which has been consistent in the stand it has taken.
I wish to refer to statements made in the house by the then member for Medicine Hat, Mr. Mitchell, who, incidentally, is now a major in Canada's active army. Referring to those of our group on September 11, 1939, he said:
The new democracy group has laid down the principle in Canada and in this house that when Canada^ is at war the whole of Canada is at war. You cannot conscript men and have industry and finance volunteer. You cannot conscript finance and industry and have men volunteer. This is a sound principle; it is an elementary principle of good business which it would seem imperative for this parliament to accept, if we choose not to do so now, circumstances will eventually compel us to do so. I sound this solemn note of warning to the government, that we cannot afford not to begin right. The experience of the last war, if it taught us anything, taught us that. Why is it that we refuse to learn? Must we in this crisis repeat the initial blunders and wastage of resources

The Budget-Mr. Shaw
and man-power that took place in the last war? If we must, then let us decide to do it frankly and openly; let us not pretend that we are not doing it. But if we would learn from the experience of the last war, then let us face the matter frankly and clearly now', and admit that the answer lies in national service-not national service of men alone, of finance alone or of industry alone; anything less than national service of all three together as Canadians would be a supreme demonstration of inefficiency.
And then, the next few lines:
The government have declared against universal conscription; the Conservative opposition have officially declared themselves as against universal conscription; the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation have declared against universal conscription. This means that these parties are allied on a principle which means suicide for Canada.
Dealing with the word "conscription" I wish to read just one paragraph from the speech delivered by the hon. member for Lethbridge in the same debate. He was referring to conscription, as it applied to manpower,- and said:
Let us look at what the wrord means to-day. Consult your dictionary and you will find all it means is forceful enrolment of men or money that they might be available for use at the discretion of the government. It does not necessarily mean that every man conscripted will don khaki, or that he will appear in the battle lines of the world. It does mean that he shall be available to be placed where, in the opinion of those in charge, he might best serve his country. Who hesitates to be placed in that position? I do not.
It should not be necessary for me to quote further from the official record. We resent very much the attempt on the part of some people, at different times, to ally this group with them in the attitude which they adopted toward this whole question, not only before the outbreak of war, but actually after the outbreak.
More than that, I think there is one other purpose served. Sometimes we find spokesmen for certain groups, who to-day justifiably feel very much ashamed1 of the stand they took over the years, endeavouring to say, since they have changed their stand: "This is what we have always stood for." I say with considerable emphasis that we are the only ones who can claim to have been consistent from the start.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What does the hon. member say about my own stand?

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am speaking of our group, as a group. True, there are some individuals who may have taken a consistent stand. My references have been made to groups.
There is another matter to which I find it necessary to make reference this afternoon. It does not always please me to have to
100-296i
make these references, but sometimes we have no choice. I refer to certain statements made by the leader of the C.C.F. party during a recent press interview. The hon. member, referring to the Social Credit party-and I think he was making special reference to the government of Alberta-said, according to the headlines, which are more or less confirmed by the text, if he was reported correctly- "Social Credit on Way Out-Coldwell". I take no exception to that, because I say we are on our way out-to demonstrate that we are capable of rocking their candidates back on their heels as they have never been rocked before.
One amazing thing in connection with the interview was that there seemed to be a certain amount of ill feeling on the part of the leader of that group in that we had not sought his advice before calling an election in Alberta. He seemed to indicate that there was a degree of indecent haste. Let me point out to him that wherever by-elections have not been held in Canada he has taken a prominent part in actually seeking redress in the courts, or has encouraged others to do so. Moreover,, where certain provincial governments have extended their normal lifetime, he has been most vociferous in his contention that this procedure was undemocratic. The Social Credit government in the province of Alberta will have completed four years and four months in office by the time of the election. We are giving the people an opportunity to express their views. We feel that it is inopportune and improper to impugn motives in connection with the holding of an election. The leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party in Alberta for a period of months before the four years were completed endeavoured to convince the people there that we were afraid of an election, that we were afraid to go out and seek a mandate from the people. Then almost immediately after our announcement of an election he cried to high heaven that there was trickery somewhere, that there was indecent haste.
I do not like to do this, but I must reply to the further charge that we have carried on against what he called the democratic policies of the C.C.F. In this house, in the province of Alberta and across Canada we have endeavoured to point out to the people the dangers which exist. We are very much opposed to a rigidly regimented economy, and we are not at all backward about making those facts known. We base our fears upon the statements of certain persons whom we regard as being authorities. I have made an analysis
The Budget-Mr. Shaw

of the publication "Social Planning for Canada" put out under the auspices of the League for Social Reconstruction, which I -believe is regarded as -the Canadian socialist organization.
I should like to draw attention to the authors of this publication. They include Eugene Forsey, J. King Gordon, Doctor Leonard Marsh, J. F. Parkington, F. R. Scott, Graham Spry and Frank H. Underhill. I should like to quote from page 227 of that publication, where it says:
If we want planning, then "we", that is, the generality of Canadians, have to delegate the task of formulating and administering a plan to some particular group or groups of men. These men will have great power over the lives and fortunes of their fellow citizens.
That is the type of thing we are opposed to. There is altogether too much governmental meddling in the affairs of our people. Then I quote from page 493 of the same publication:
Every time we set up a new permanent independent commission to carry on some function of government, we deny in practice the naive theory of democracy in which we still profess to believe-that all power lies with the "peepul" to be exercised by their elected representatives.
We as social crediters certainly do not subscribe to that. Then I quote from page 225:
Wide powers placed in the hands of a central planning board undoubtedly involve the possibility of interference with personal initiative and freedom.
We are very much opposed to any such proposition as that. We' do not wish to have a greater amount of interference with the personal initiative and freedom of our people. Then I go to page 494, where it states:
The proposals for economic reconstruction which have been set forth in this book will certainly, if they are adopted, strengthen both of the tendencies which have just been discussed-the growth of the power of the executive at the expense of the power of the legislature, and the extension of the practice of government by independent experts.
Here is another one to which we take the most violent exception. This outlines the philosophy of life which some are trying to bring about in this country. I quote from page 225:
National planning is also important as a very real step towards the realization of that international control.
I quote these to give the house a complete picture of the things to which we are opposed, no matter by whom they are advocated. I turn to page 498 where it states:
And if a socialist, government coming into office in a period of emergency seeks power to

proceed by order in council without day to day reference to the bouse, it will only be doing what -has been already done in both England and Canada by those bulwarks of constitutional traditions, Conservative or "National" governments.
There is a clear-cut indication that these people are prepared to adopt a policy of government by order in council as a permanent-feature of our Canadian life. I should like to quote from another publication, " Democracy Needs Socialism." I could hardly believe this one, which readis:
The introduction of inventions could' foe controlled if great displacement of labour is apt to result.
That one just about stunned me, because it is a clear-cut indication that if the introduction of inventions affects in any way the putting to work of all our people, those inventions will be controlled. I do not know whether the leader of the C.C.F. party subscribes to what is contained in that book, but I do know that many of those writers are associated with bis movement. I see F. R. Scott and Eugene Forsey listed, and what is remarkable, in view of our social security proposal, is that I see also the name of Doctor Leonard Marsh.
I should like to refer to another paragraph in " Social Planning for Canada " which indicates that those who are responsible for writing the book are fully in accord with the present financial system. I quote from pages 286 and 2S7 as follows:
Anxious to provide the victims of depression with a scapegoat, the monetary cranks-
Referring to us, I suppose.
-have nominated the banks for the position, by means of oversimplification or fallacious analysis of the nature of our economic system, they assert that the cause of our difficulties lies in the contraction of credit. Or in the debt-creating system, or in the "gold racket" or whatnot-with all of which it is easy to identify the hanker.
While the men responsible for the writing of this book may he willing to adopt a change in the ownership of the bank, they assert that they do not propose to make any fundamental change in the system of banking.
AVe have said as social crediters that socialism is anti-Christian. I know that is a strong statement, but I know also that all I need to do is to quote from the official publications of the socialists in order to show their views in that regard. A declaration was made at the 1912 convention of the American socialist party-I have never heard any repudiation of this-that the ethics of socialism and religion are directly opposed to each other. I should like to quote from "The Ethics of Socialism," by Belfort Bax, as follows:

The Budget-Mr. Esling
The association of Christianism with any form of socialism is a mystery. No good socialist can be a Christian.
Then I desire to quote Liebnecht, who happens to be a German socialist, and who says
It is our duty as socialists to root out the faith in God with all our might. Nor is any one worthy of the name who does not consecrate himself to the spread of atheism.
Then I should like to quote Professor Karl Pearson, an English socialist, as follows:
Can a greater gulf be imagined than really exists between the current Christianity and the socialistic code?
Then in "Science of Political Economy" Henry George says this:
Modern socialism is without religion and its tendency is atheistic.
I could go on to quote a number of others, but I think what I have quoted demonstrates the fundamental reason why we have opposed socialism, why our organization in all parts of Canada has opposed socialism. If the publication "Social Planning for Canada" means anything, then as a party who oppose centralization, who oppose regimentation, who oppose greater government interference with the lives of our people, we could not do otherwise than to oppose, with all the vehemence at our command, socialism or any form of totalitarianism. So that when the leader of the C.C.F. states that we are carrying on a radio and press campaign against fundamental democratic policies of the C.C.F., he has to do a bit of explaining, because our campaign has been against those very things which I have read as typical of certain of the leading socialists in Canada. If he wishes to ally himself with what is said in "Social Planning for Canada", then of course we shall have to admit that we have been carrying on a press and radio campaign against the C.C.F. I do not like to make any further reference to this matter, and I shall not do so. It is not very often that we find it desirable to take a course of action such as I have taken to-day, but at the same time we certainly are not prepared to sit down and gobble up all that some people are prepared to hand to us on whatever type of platter they may desire to use for the purpose.
As to the amendment to the budget, we find it unnecessary to take exception to the first five paragraphs of the Progressive Conservative amendment. We find that the intent of those five paragraphs is deserving of oui support. The next paragraph, paragraph (f) is susceptible of a number of interpretations. However, we feel that the value of the amendment outweighs its weaker and less desirable features, and we are therefore prepared, Mr. Speaker, to support the amendment.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members have made a very general review of the budget at this session, but one can hardly overlook the fact that the budget contains no suggestion of ways and means of providing for a broad comprehensive programme of employment in the post-war days. After all is said and done, it is employment that the ordinary man wants, whether he be war veteran or civilian. It is true that there is provision for vocational and technical training and for some special education. But the average wage-earner wants a scale of wages which will permit him to provide for his family the comforts of a modem home and the educational facilities enjoyed by his more favoured neighbour. He wants his children to be brought up to have the same advantages as the children of his neighbour.
Perhaps the most generous source of wealth and of employment lies in the development of the products of the forest, of the sea, of the soil and of the mines. But the mines differ from all these other sources of wealth and of employment. When the forests are denuded of their products, nature replenishes them, and so it is with the sea. When the soil gets run down, its fertility can be restored by fertilizer. But the wealth that is taken from the mines is taken for good. It can never be replaced. There is no such thing as reproduction of minerals.
I judge that every one of the ministers has received from the Canadian Mining Institute, and from every mining association across Canada, and from the various communities in which mines are located, briefs and appeals for a revision of mining legislation and of mining taxation, for the very reason that there is so much risk in the investment of funds in mining companies. There is no telling whether you are ever going to get your money back from a mine. The hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) the other day presented to the house in detail his technical reasons as a mining engineer, and other reasons gained from his experience, as to why there should be a revision of mining taxation if mining development throughout Canada is to continue. He spoke as a mining engineer. I want to endorse his proposals speaking from the experience of half a century in the mining districts of West Kootenay. I speak from personal observations.
Early in 1900, as the British Columbia Gazetteer states there were 2,500 registered mining companies in British Columbia. We will admit that some of the mining properties
The Budget-Mr. Esling

had experienced did its work, and the men became physically disabled. When they applied for pension the medical sheet was referred to and they were told that they were discharged as A-l and that the disability for which pension was asked was due to post-war services.
I have seen a disabled veteran stand before the tribunal, supported by the soldiers' advocate and by his own attending physician. He was unable to stand alone. Naturally one would be justified in assuming that that was due to exposure or shell shock or some overseas service, but he was told that he was discharged as physically fit, in category I, and could get no pension. But I shall tell you what the Consolidated Mining and Smelting company did in the case of that veteran. They put him in a wheel chair at the gate. They let him sit there and take messages from those who chose to enter, but he received no pension or assistance from the government. Therefore I think the greatest service that the relatives of friends of a man overseas can do for him, or that the government can do for him, is to advise any boy overseas to be sure that there is a most detailed record of every incident in connection with his services; any time he was in the hospital or wounded or had any disability whatsoever should show on his record so that when he is demobilized and receives his medical chart he has some grounds on which to make a future application for pension if he needs it.
I wish to return to the Minister of Finance for just a moment. In July of last year I brought to the attention of the government the fact that so many deaf and hard of hearing people were penalized because the high price of a hearing aid was beyond their financial reach. Those hearing aids sold for $150 to $200. I asked the government to have the Research Council of Canada go into this matter to determine what was a fair price at which those instruments could be manufactured. Well, they did not do that. What happened was this. It rested with a manufacturer in the United States to call in his research council. He told them to produce a hearing aid which would be within the reach of the general public, and I am glad to say that while those hearing aids at $40 were being distributed to veterans and paid for by the Department of Pensions and National Health, it was only last week that the same company opened its office in Windsor, Ontario, so that the deaf and hard of hearing people in Canada could secure that device at the same price in Canadian funds at which it is sold in the United States, namely, $40. The war exchange

tax and the sales tax are paid and it is delivered to the buyer's home.

While I am on this subject I should like to ask the Minister of Finance if he will not just interest himself in this, and give thought to the fact that there are so many deaf and hard of hearing people who cannot carry on any vocation whatsoever unless they have a hearing aid. I wish to ask him if he will not provide for an allowance or a deduction in income tax for hearing aids and for the cost of maintaining the batteries, just as allowances for maintenance are made in the department of pensions. He might choose one of two things. If he makes that allowance, it permits people to earn their living. Deaf people and blind people can earn just as good a living, if they have the opportunity, as sighted people, but they must have help. The minister will have to choose between making that allowance or losing income tax from such people when they are helped into gainful occupations.

The Budget-Mr. Black (Cumberland)
I cannot see whether the Prime Minister is in his seat, but I wish to refer to the fact that I think it was last March I asked the Minister of Labour if the Japanese would be removed from the interior of British Columbia when hostilities ceased. He said that that was a matter in which it would be necessary for the government to determine as a future policy. I know that it is a matter in which one cannot jump to conclusions too readily, for the reason that there are international complications; but the Minister of National Defence during the absence of the Prime Minister at the conference in the old country stated that during this session the Prime Minister would make a statement as to the policy in connection with the Japanese. Well, the war has been going on for five years. This is a serious question, and I am just wondering whether we can keep these Japanese interned after hostilities end. If we cannot; if we must simply lift the bars and let them out, they are going to invade the business districts of Kootenay and the adjoining constituency of Yale. It may be said they can be sent to other provinces, but after the war there will be nothing to keep them there. They will come back to British Columbia and congregate wherever they please. I believe the government would receive popular approval if it took steps to deport these people. I do not mean that those born in Canada should be deported; that would be contrary to our constitution, which must be respected. I do not mean that those who have been naturalized should be deported, unless it can be shown that they were naturalized for improper motives; and most of them were naturalized for the sole purpose of getting a fishing licence. I do say that the nationals of Japan, for whom this country has no responsibility, who owe allegiance to the emperor of Japan, should be deported, and that they should be encouraged to take with them such others as may be willing to go.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know it is the desire that this debate be terminated, and I do not wish to prolong it. I have been in Ottawa since about the middle of January, and it is now well on to the middle of July. Those of us who come from the outlying portions of Canada, particularly coming from Nova Scotia, want to be back home for part of the summer months. There are many matters having to do with the maritime provinces that should be discussed, but I am going to deal with only one or two this afternoon.
I want to bring to the attention of the house and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) one matter of very great importance, which I do
not believe has received the attention it deserves. I refer to the unfair taxation on electrical energy in Canada. I cannot understand why a system of taxation should be continued under which the central provinces are largely exempted, great public utilities are exempted, but smaller plants, all financed by private enterprise, are subjected to very heavy taxation. A short time ago Premier Godbout delivered an address in which he explained his action in taking over the Montreal Light, Heat and Power company, taking credit to himself for saving the people of Quebec very large amounts of money in federal taxation on the generation of electrical energy in Quebec. Any system of taxation on electrical service should have some basis of fairness to the companies producing the electricity, to the municipalities, the industries and the householders consuming it. Such is not the case in Canada to-day. Taxation should be adjusted so that the production of electrical energy may be encouraged, in order that rural electrification may be carried out as extensively as possible, to make electricity available to farmers and others in outlying districts. Why should electrical energy generated at great natural water power sites, financed by public money borrowed at low rates of interest, be free of taxation, while smaller plants, privately owned, are forced to pay heavy taxes? There is nothing fair or just in that.
I want to quote from the address by Mr. Godbout, as reported in the Montreal newspapers of June 29:
For household service the customer in a great city like Montreal paid $1.80 for power kilowatt hours, while the consumer in Toronto only paid $1.31. In St. Johns, Quebec, the cost was $2.10, while at Kitchener it was scarcely $1.24. . . .
For industrial and commercial services the difference was even more marked. Electrical consumption, which would have cost $97 in Toronto, a centre served by the Ontario hydro, would have cost $420 in Montreal and $510 in St. Johns. . . .
Well, the hydro has put an end to the ridiculous regime I have described. It has already reduced the rates by $2,210,000 a year in the district of Montreal alone, and three other hydro electric companies have followed in reducing their rates by more than a million dollars. The hydro has been able to do this because it is relieved of the federal tax of six millions a year. . . .
This has been accomplished because hydro Quebec was not created to benefit the provincial treasury, but to service the customers at cheap rates and permit us to complete as soon as possible the urgently needed rural electrification. The service as such has not changed. . . .
In Nova Scotia part of our electrical energy is generated by publicly-owned plants, and part

The Budget-Mr. Black (Cumberland)
Dy private industry. Some communities pay heavy federal taxation on their electricity, while others escape such taxes. The people of Nova Scotia pay more than $1,000,000 a year because of this inequitable basis of taxation. I should like to read an extract from an article which appeared in the Halifax Herald as late as June 30, in connection with some publicity having to do with inquiries into the rates on electrical service. Due to war conditions there has been increased production and consumption of electrical energy, which automatically reduces rates:
Nova Scotia's position in the utility field is peculiar. Many of the plants are publicly owned and are exempt from federal and provincial taxation. On the other hand the biggest are in private hands and subject 'to levies :by Ottawa, which amount to a sum in excess of a million dollars a year. The remainder is the municipal and provincial taxation paid by these same companies.
I have made inquiries in my own constituency of Cumberland, where practically all the electrical energy is generated by private industry. About forty years ago a company established in that county the first electrical generating plant in the world at the mouth of a coal mine, utilizing refuse coal. This plant has been relocated, enlarged and modernized, so that it can compete as to cost with all but the largest of the hydro generating plants. To-day, however, enterprise is penalized and householders and industries depending upon this plant have to pay fifty per cent extra to provide for taxes. I wired the manager of that company, as follows:
Please wire me amount federal and provincial taxes during last year paid by your company, also estimate total amount such taxes paid in Cumberland. What percentage could rates be reduced if all such taxes were exempted?
This is the reply, dated July 3:
Provincial and federal taxes total $106,800; equal 21 per cent gross revenue. Municipal taxes in addition $19,900, equal 3-9 per cent. These do not include 8 per cent federal sales tax on lighting. Edison Company, Springhill, tax probably $12,000.
There is another privately operated light and power company generating electricity and serving the eastern portion of my constituency and the northern portion of the county of Colchester. All the companies in Cumberland, and a large number of those in Nova Scotia, are called upon to pay heavy federal and provincial taxes, while the electrical generating plants in central Canada escape.
There is no justification whatsoever for the continuance of a tax, when it is not levied equitably on the people in all sections of the country. There is no justification at all for imposing heavy taxation upon private enter-

prise established in pioneer days, and because of economies and efficiency in operation is now producing electrical energy so as to compete with government plants. Still these companies are taxed, and their charges are from 33i to 50 per cent higher than they would be if government taxes were not imposed.
I bring this matter to the attention of the minister, the house and country, and request that in view of the fact that the taxes on electrioal energy are not now levied throughout Canada on an equitable basis, and are unfair and unjust to many communities, these conditions should not be allowed to continue. A special amendment should be made to the budget resolutions in order that all federal taxation and, following that, all provincial taxation, be taken off the generation and distribution of electricity, so that people in all parts of Canada will be treated alike, and so that there may be a wider use of electrical energy in connection with rural electrification, and the establishment and operation of small industries.
I hope the minister and the government will accept my recommendation. Certainly in fairness to people throughout Canada no taxation should be tolerated when it is levied on the present basis, whereby the premier of a province can make an appeal to his electors on the ground that he has been able to take over a big utility and. because he is no longer compelled to pay any tax to the federal government, he is in a position to relieve the people of that province to the amount of $6,000,000, while smaller industries elsewhere are compelled to continue payment of these taxes. I make this appeal to the minister to see that this taxation is cancelled, so that all parts of Canada may be treated alike.
There are many other matters to which I should like to refer. I would speak particularly about conditions in the coal mines of Nova Scotia. A serious statement was made only a few days ago by the minister of mines of Nova Scotia, Hon. Mr. Currie, when he gave warning to the people of that province and the people of Canada, that if the cost of producing coal in Nova Scotia continues at its present level we will have seen the end of the coal-mining industry in eastern Canada. I hope that production can be increased and costs reduced.
I believe the discontent among miners and absenteeism can be traced largely to what they consider to be unfairness in taxation. I believe there is a general feeling among miners that taxation is excessive and unfair. If the proposals made in the amendment moved by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) are acted upon, it will
The Budget-Mr. Gray don
have a very beneficial effect upon the morale of the people working in the mines, shipbuilding and war industries. They would no longer be subject to taxation on overtime. The taxation on single persons would begin at $800, and on married persons, at $1,600.
It is very important that this change be made, and that we assist in this way in building up the morale of workers in all parts of Canada. I feel that the amendment would have a very beneficial effect on the coal mining industry in my province, and I shall heartily support it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wonder if I might at this time have only two or three minutes. I have no desire to make a speech, but there are one or two things I should like to bring to the attention of the house.
In order that the Progressive Conservatives' position on the man-power problem shall be made incapable of the kind of misrepresentation attached to it by government supporters during the current debate and certain hostile sections of the press, I now reassert and reaffirm our policy relative to this vital issue.
It is clearly and unmistakably declared in the Winnipeg platform which reads as follows:
5. Recognizing that the world struggle in which Canada is engaged requires a total /war effort, we believe in compulsory national selective service, and that all those selected to serve in the armed forces should be available for service wherever required. We believe in the effective total utilization and proper allocation for war, by compulsion where necessary, of all the resources of Canada, including agriculture, industry and finance, as well as man-power, and that our aim should be at all times to bring about so far as human means can achieve it, an equality in sacrifice.
It has been reaffirmed by our national leader on such important occasions as the meetings at Massey hall, Toronto, a year ago and subsequently in the city of Quebec and elsewhere. It has been redeclared over and over in the House of Commons during this session and previous ones.
The statement of the director of national selective service that Canada was headed into the most acute labour shortage the country has ever faced, coupled with the urgent appeals for reinforcements made by the director of recruiting, at a time when our troops overseas were fighting to gain a bridgehead in Normandy, were followed by a speech by the national chairman of our party at Guelph, Ontario, on June 19 last.
At the same meeting the national leader of our party made this statement at the close of the national chairman's address, and this is what Mr. Bracken said:
One point in particular in Mr. McTague's remarks I wish to support and endorse. He pointed out that since the war we have had many statements from the Department of National Defence as to the urgency of reinforcements, and he added, "Surely national honour demands that without an hour's delay the necessary order in council should be passed making these reinforcements available." In this time of national emergency, surely there will be no Canadians who wall find it in their hearts to deny that appeal. Certainly it carries the endorsement of this party, and I would like to think of the great majority of people in all parties as well.
The Winnipeg platform was further followed by the financial critic of our party in this debate, as well as by those on our side who have spoken. It is incorporated in the amendment now before the house, which was moved and will be unanimously supported by our party. In other words, the policy adopted at Winnipeg is the policy of the Progressive Conservative party; and in accord with it I now call upon the government to pass immediately the order in council making the home defence army available for service anywhere and demand that the mobilization call-up be applied equally to the end that equality of service shall be achieved in all parts of Canada.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this late date in the debate I do not intend to delay the house very long, but I think I should say a few words. So far as the constituency which I represent, Yukon, is concerned, the effect of the budget will not be very great. There will be a slight reduction in taxation of those in the lower income brackets. Before the war the income of the people of the Yukon was derived almost entirely from the mining of gold and silver. As I have stated before in this house, the recent high taxation, probably necessary because of the war, has made it very difficult for Yukoners to carry on. This high taxation added to the high cost of living makes it doubly hard for them.
As has happened in many parts of Canada, the war has brought what might be termed a measure of prosperity to southern Yukon. The United States have undertaken a number of projects up there, such as the Alaska highway, the piping of oil from Norman Wells, the establishment and operation of an oil refinery at Whitehorse, and the building of a splendid airport there by Canada. These have all added to the prosperity of that part of the territory. They have all entailed the expenditure of large sums of money, which has meant increased revenues to merchants, hotelkeepers, contractors and possibly to most of the general public.

The Budget-Mr. Black (Yukon)
As I have said before in this house, the government policy of establishing wage ceilings in the Yukon on Canadian employers and employees while United States employers and employees, working side by side with them in Yukon, were allowed to pay and receive much higher wages, has created a great and lasting dissatisfaction. At the last session I urged the government either to remove the ceiling on wages in Yukon or to make foreign employers and employees conform to the rates established by this government while in Canada. However, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) turned a deaf ear to the suggestion, and the unfairness to Canadian labour has continued.
The shortage of man-power has handicapped gold mining in Yukon, as it has throughout Canada. The shortage of man-power in Yukon is due to the fact that most of the young men there who were of war age quickly answered their country's call and are now to be found in the navy, the army and the air force on all the fighting fronts of the world. Due to high taxation and the shortage of manpower the output of gold in Yukon for the current year will not be more than one-third of the average production.
In order to show the effect of the government's taxation policy on mining in Canada I should like to quote from studies which have been made by competent authorities and which show that Canada's mining industry is in a precarious position. New mines are not being developed fast enough to replace those being worked out. Eighty-four per cent of Canada's 1942 metal production came from mineral areas discovered prior to 1920, and only five per cent came from mineral areas discovered since 1930. That is a serious state of affairs. The report of the committee on reconstruction appointed by the dominion government says of the mining industry:
An immediate radical change of national policy in regard to mining is clearly indicated in order for us to pull our weight in the war and to have a reasonable chance of maintaining a mining industry in the post-war period. If this policy is not changed there is little use in counting on the mining industry to help carry the post-war load or to help in the rehabilitation of our men now in war services.
The Canadian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy, in an official brief on taxation presented to the federal government on February 24, 1944, said:
Unless relief from destructive taxation is forthcoming :at an early date, the Canadian mining industry will continue, at an accelerated pace, on the road to exhaustion.

The brief on taxation of the Quebec metal and asbestos mining industries emphasizes:
The immediate future of the Canadian mining industry, and the part it may or may not play in post-war years an alleviating unemployment and the_ rehabilitation of other industries, is largely in the hands of the dominion government. On it must rest the responsibility. Drastic and prompt action by federal authorities is necessary provided the industry is to-survive.
The Ontario mining association brief says:
To-day, mining in Canada is on a salvage basis, with little or nothing being done to assure its continuance as an all-important basic industry.
The Ontario mining commission, appointed by the province, declares in its preliminary report:
Unless some favourable action is taken to overcome the handicaps under which the business is now operating, it will continue its present decline, and at an accelerated rate.
The Canadian mining industry does not ask preferential treatment as to taxes. Nor is it the aim of the mining industry to attempt to shift the necessarily heavy war-time tax load on to other shoulders. What the mining industry does ask, however, is that mining taxation be placed on a sound basis, and it recommends:
That depletion allowance of fifty per cent of the net earnings of metal and industrial mineral mines be allowed, and extended to dividends paid by such mines.
That taxes paid annually to provincial governments and to municipalities be allowed as a deduction from earnings of all mining companies before assessment for dominion income and/or excess profits tax purposes.
That all annual expenditures made by mining companies on outside exploration in any part of Canada, excepting cost of options or purchases of property, be allowed as a deduction from -earnings before assessment for dominion income and/or excess profits tax.
I am informed that the above recommendations represent the unanimous views of all investigating bodies appointed by government and industry alike as to the proper method of providing an over-all equitable plan of mining taxation and to place the industry on a footing where it will best be able to perpetuate itself to the lasting benefit of Canada.
In last year's budget, part of the amounts contributed by corporations and syndicates to be expended in exploration and prospecting were credited on taxation. In Yukon, not only corporations but individuals contribute to prospecting and exploration, but under the budget of last year the contributions by individuals were not allowed as credits so far as taxation was concerned. I wrote to the Minister of Finance suggesting that his policy be broadened, and he referred me to the Minister

The Budget-Mr. Black (Yukon)
[DOT]of National Revenue. Since then I have had the privilege of briefly discussing it with that minister, and I am inclined to think he is favourably impressed and that some relief will be granted.
A wide range of subjects has been discussed in this budget debate, but one which I think is of public interest, one which should be of interest to the house and the people of Canada, is the present unsettled condition of the civil service of Canada, a condition which has obtained throughout the past four years. My attention was called to this matter by a recent broadcast by Raburn. Instead of the claims and grievances of the civil service employees being referred as they should be to the civil service commission I understand that the Minister of Finance has undertaken by his *own efforts to a large extent to deal with these complaints and difficulties and that a national joint council on civil service affairs, consisting of sixteen members, has been appointed. It is not to be headed by the chairman of the civil service commission, who I think would be best fitted for the position, but by one with only a limited experience in civil service matters. As yet I do not think the house has been told, at any rate for my part I do not yet understand, what the functions of this national council on civil service affairs are to be. Is the council to supplant the civil sendee commission? Is it to take over their duties? If so, I think it would be necessary to have an amendment to the Civil Service Act.
I think the house should- be informed of the activities of the government concerning the civil service commission and the civil service generally. When the Civil Service Act was first passed it was considered to be the finest piece of civil service legislation in existence. Under it the returned soldiers were given a preference which satisfied them and was equitable, and for a long time the civil service commission saw to it that a member of the Canadian Legion sat on every board of civil service examiners. The civil service was reclassified by the commission on a duty-salary basis and on the readjustment the additional salaries paid to the civil service in Canada amounted to $10,000,000. I believe that the returned men of to-day would not have that well-established system abolished- or interfered with. But my information is that the civil service commission since the war began has been largely ignored and that thousands of so-called war workers have wormed their way into the civil service without reference to the civil service commission. Take the Bank of Canada, with its army of employees; the income tax branch, with its army of employees;
the broadcasting corporation and the unemployment insurance commission-my information is that none of these employees is subject to control by the civil service commission. New departments, new agencies, numerous special so-called war departments and agencies are being established, and my information is that the civil service commission is not consulted in regard to any of them. In fact, the civil service commission has become a joke and is ignored.
In the past the civil service commission and the civil service were looked upon as the right hand of the government. The civil service will have increased duties and responsibilities after the war and it should be strengthened and encouraged. As I see it, the policies of all parties should be: hands off the civil service. Positions for returned men which are now being filled by others should be reserved for the returned men. Only recently a radio broadcast from the civil service commission announced the establishment of some new agency and that the age limit for the employees of that agency would be sixty years. Heretofore the age limit was thirty-five years. Why that change of policy?
I think it would not be asking too much if I asked the Minister of Finance before the close of the session, if not in closing this debate, to tell the house of proposed changes in the civil service and in the civil service commission and of the reports that have been made to him or to the government by, I think, three commissions or committees which have been set up on civil service matters.
Canada is progressing in social legislation, which is all to the good, but the cost of administration of that social legislation may not be realized by some members of this house, much less by the people of Canada who pay the shot. For instance, take the unemployment insurance commission. In the present fiscal year it will cost over $5,000,000 in federal taxes to pay the expenses of the unemployment insurance commission. This is more than twice as much as the commission has paid in workers' benefits in the previous three years. Administration costs or expenses during those three years were almost five times as great as the total amount paid in benefits. Workers' benefits to the end of March last totalled $2,465,043.41. Administration costs for the same period totalled $12,187,993.64. These administration expenses come out of taxes and are an extra charge on the insurance contributor. I am all in favour of unemployment insurance, but surely it could be administered and handled at a lesser cost to the taxpayers of Canada.
The Budget-Mr. llsley

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think there are many other speakers, so that I will say what I have to say now, in the hope that we can take the division or divisions this afternoon.
The debate has gone on for some days. I am sorry that it has not been possible for me to be in the house all the time, but I have kept very closely in touch with the debate. It will be impossible for me, of course, to deal with all the suggestions that have been made. Two amendments have been proposed, the first by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), and then a subamendment by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). The subamendment proposed by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was an addition to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe. That is, it placed the stamp of C.C.F. approval upon the proposals of the Progressive Conservative amendment, and then added a few proposals peculiar to the C.C.F.
That subamendment was voted on at a very early stage of the debate without any discussion, but since most of the remarks of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar were made before he moved his amendment, I should like to deal with some features of his speech.
I am going to take the position that the amendment proposed by the Progressive Conservative party contains certain inconsistencies and evidences a degree of irresponsibility; but I would not go quite that far in regard to the C.C.F. amendment. Irresponsible-yes; that is, irresponsible from the point of view of those who would like to see the framework of society as we have constructed it in Canada continued, but not inconsistent. To those who believe that business should be torn to pieces and that class antagonisms should be aroused to that end the amendment is a good amendment, and the speech of the hon. gentleman is a good speech and is consistent with the doctrine of the party which believes those things. But to those who believe that a good part of what we built in the past we should continue to retain, the amendment of course would not commend itself, nor would the speech.

Since I have been in the house I have heard a great many criticisms of budgets, and I have often heard this phrase, which was used by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, "rich man's budget." He used it in the concluding part of his remarks. Let me read to the house his words as reported in Hansard, at page 4353:
I feel that this is indeed a rich man's budget. It offers a sop to the poor and underprivileged, but on the other hand it contains most valuable concessions to the rich and powerful individuals and corporations who to-day control this land. That, Mr. Speaker, is what I wanted to say.
I cannot for a moment let these remarks pass unchallenged. I consider them entirely unjustified. It seems to me that any person who regards any budget which has been brought down during the course of this war as a rich man's budget has something wrong with his judgment. The budgets which we have presented to this parliament during the war have imposed very steeply graduated progressive taxation upon the people of Canada, have taken enormous taxes out of those with the higher incomes and those of wealth. That has been the policy which has been followed throughout the war. To adopt this old catch-phrase of a "rich man's budget" and tack it on to this budget is not in keeping with the sense of responsibility which the leader of a group or a party in this house should have.
"Big business" was the phrase which the hon. gentleman used; we were helping big business, he said. He left out of account altogether the fact that the means of encouragement which are proposed in this budget to business in this country, the assurances we are giving to business as to what it can expect in the post-war period and in the transition period, are privileges available not only to industry but to agriculture; they are available not only to big business but to small business; and they are a means of encouragement which we are giving for the purpose of providing employment and helping the rank and file of the common people of this country to make a suitable transition from the war period to the post-war period and to prosperity in the post-war period.
The hon. gentleman said something else in his speech which I should like to criticize. He said, as reported in Hansard, at page 4349:
The 'present concentration of wealth in their hands-
He is speaking about the speculators and the big holders who, he says, will be taking up the cashed bonds after the war.
-will in my opinion after the war be intensified because our present taxation methods make that almost certain. With this and other factors in mind the party which I have the honour to

The Budget-Mr. llsley
represent have proposed that the government guarantee victory bonds to the extent of one hundred cents on the dollar for the protection of the small holders against depreciation or speculation.
Now, will the present concentration of wealth-if any-in the hands of big holders of bonds be intensified because our present taxation methods make that almost certain? I challenge that statement, and I want to deal with it. It is true, I believe, although I have never checked the figures, that after the last war there was a tendency to concentration of victory bonds in the hands of big holders. But there have been two changes in our taxation system between that time and this which set in motion directly opposite forces. The first is that our income tax now taxes all the income from bonds. At the end of the last war, with a large number of the bonds issued during the war tax-free as to income, they took on a value in the hands of persons in receipt of heavy incomes which caused them to become concentrated in their hands. That is not the case at the present time. The case is just the reverse, because persons with large incomes, if they acquire victory bonds after this war, will have to pay a very large percentage-sometimes as high as eighty, ninety, or ninety-five per cent of the income which they receive on these bonds-by way of taxation, and concentration will be discouraged, instead of encouraged as it was by the taxation arrangements in existence before.
The other change in our taxation system between the last war and this is the change in succession duties. Succession duties are much higher. They are much higher in the provinces, and we have dominion succession duties as well.
The combined effect of the three factors- the factor of taxability of all victory bond interest, the factor of steeply progressive rates and very much higher rates of taxation on victory bond interest than was the case before, and the factor of succession duties- will make for dispersal rather than concentration, a fact to which the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has given no consideration whatever.
Now as to the next statement:
With this and other factors in mind the party which I have the honour to represent have proposed that the government guarantee victory bonds to the extent of one hundred cents on the dollar for the protection of the small holders against depreciation or speculation.
The effect of that proposal which the hon. gentleman has made, and made repeatedly, and which has a certain plausibility, is simply
this, that no person would have any reason for accepting or buying a bond which paid less than three per cent. It would be utterly impracticable, utterly impossible to make a division between small holders and large holders. Any provision that if more than a certain value of bonds were presented the guarantee would not apply would be entirely impracticable; and if the guarantee were applied to all bonds, why would anyone buy a treasury bill or lend money on a deposit certificate or lend money for two years to the government? They would all buy the long-term bonds at three per cent, because their par value would be guaranteed throughout, and the result would be that we would lose millions of dollars every year, the advantage which we now get through our market for short-term securities.
These are very simple considerations, and I am greatly surprised that the leader of the C.C.F. party, occupying so responsible a position, should repeat and repeat this policy of his of guaranteeing that the bonds would always remain at par, having no regard whatever to the cost of financing which that would entail on the country. I have not very much more to say about the speech of the leader of the C.C.F. party. I think it was consistent with the attitude of the C.C.F. toward business and the economic problems of this country.
I now wish to direct some attention to the amendment proposed by the Progressive Conservative party. Before I come to that may I say that in the course of this debate some hon. members have expressed a considerable amount of concern at the size of the debt and the degree to which it is mounting. One of the hon. members who spoke very forcibly on this subject was the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. McGeer). I think he believes that we should have financed the war in an entirely different way, a way which would not have resulted in the piling up of the volume of internal debt that has been necessary under our present method of financing. I have gone into that question time after time in the house, but the more I think about it, and I have thought about it quite a lot since I heard the speech of the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, the more I am convinced that we have financed the war in the only way in which any responsible government and any responsible minister would dare to finance a war, for this reason: when the government is pouring out vast sums of money on war expenditures for goods, a large proportion of which are not consumers' goods, then unless the price level is to soar to great
The Budget-Mr. Ilsley

heights the money must in some way be brought back from the people into the coffers of the country.

The surprising nature of these results is due to the fact that the government railway system was a considerable drain on government revenues in the earlier years and produced a substantial surplus last year. It may, of course, be contended that last year's Canadian National Railways surplus of $35-6 million is abnormal and could not be expected to be maintained under peace-time conditions. That may be true and hon. members are welcome to discount that factor to any extent they like. Even if we take no account whatsoever of last year's C.N.R. surplus, the net annual carrying charge of the direct and indirect 
funded debt outstanding at March 31, 1944, would be only $219-1 million, which is an increase of less than forty-seven per cent as compared with March 31, 1939, and of only about thirty-three per cent as compared with March 31, 1920. But these increases in the dollar amount of the net annual carrying charge do not reflect a corresponding increase in the weight of the burden, because they fail to take into account either the increase in population or the increase in national income or the increase in taxable capacity of the Canadian economy. If we take account of the increase in population we find* that the net

The Budget-Mr. llslev
annual carrying charge of our direct and indirect funded debt was $19 per capita in 1920 and $13.22 per capita in 1939, while to-day, even if we take no credit for the C.N.R. surplus, it is only about $18.50 per capita. More significant has been the reduction in the real burden of the public debt due to doubling or more than doubling the national income. The net annual carrying charge of our direct and indirect funded debt at March 31, 1020, was roughly 3-9 per cent of the estimated national income at that time; at March 31, 1939, it was still roughly 3-9 per cent; while at March 31, 1943, again not taking any credit for the C.N.R. surplus, it is only about 2-6 per cent of the estimated national income of to-day. Incidentally, in this connection I might point out that the annual interest charge on the British national debt in a year before the war, say 1936, was approximately five per cent of the estimated national income of the United Kingdom.
But if Canada's national income has approximately doubled since the outbreak of war, its taxable capacity has increased a good deal more. It is the surplus income over and above the cost of basic food, shelter and clothing requirements which is a significant indication of taxable capacity, and it is obvious that this surplus income has increased proportionately much more than total income. In relation, therefore, to national income, the net annual burden of Canada's direct and indirect funded debt is less than it was at the end of the last war and less than it was immediately prior to this war. In relation to taxable capacity, it is substantially less than in both previous periods.
The hon. member for Yancouver-Burrard quoted the following sentence from the annual report of the governor of the Bank of Canada:
In making these comments I do not wish to suggest that public debt could be increased at the present rate for an indefinite period without placing intolerable strain on our economy.
With that sentence I agree, but I also agree with the two following sentences in Governor Towers' report, which the hon. member failed to quote:
I do feel, however, that the war debt and the increases which will inevitably take place for a time after the war ends, can be handled without serious embarrassment. The key to this problem, as to many others, lies chiefly in the maintenance of a high level of employment and income.
I do not know whether I was justified in taking so much time in presenting these considerations to the house, but from certain hon. members I heard so much of a needlessly alarmist nature about our public debt that I thought it well for this house and the public to be told the true situation.
I now come to the speech of the hon. member for Dufferinr-Simcoe, the critic of the official opposition in respect of the budget. If the leader of the C.C.F. can be criticized for an irresponsible attitude toward business, that is an attitude which would be destructive and, according to the language he used, calculated to make an appeal on behalf of the little man against the big man-if, as I say, the leader of the C.C.F. can be criticized1 for that attitude, then certainly the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe can validly be criticized for making a speech which, in its effect, was very much of a big business or pro-business speech.
He made one very significant suggestion, namely, that, as he put it, we should eliminate double taxation in Canada. What does that mean? It means that we, now, in this year 1944 I presume, should take off altogether the corporation tax, at a time when the United States, the country which lies side by side with us, has a corporation tax. I have never fell that this was a practicable suggestion. 1 know, of course, that it is a most appealing suggestion to a great many people in the country. But make no mistake about it, the suggestion is that we take off altogether the tax on corporations, because that is the only way of which I know by which double taxation can be eliminated. That is his suggestion in this year 1944, at a time when our revenue requirements are so tremendous, and at a time when the critic of the official opposition is ostensibly laying stress upon the progressive part of the Progressive Conservative party platform, and talking on behalf of the farmers, labour and so on. That is the big suggestion he makes in his speech, that we remove the corporation tax altogether.

Something has been said about the complexity of our income tax forms. The complexity of our income tax structure and of our income tax forms is due to one thing, and one only, namely, an attempt to introduce equity in many situations. No, it is not. We could
make the income tax system just as simple

The Budget-Mr. Ilslev
as anything in the world by imposing a flat tax on everybody's income, with no exemptions. It would be so simple that no one would have any trouble in making out his tax return; but it would be unjust, it would be unsocial, it would be backward looking, it would be wrong. The complexity of our tax form and our tax methods is due largely, almost wholly, to the fact that we have tried to introduce equity into our tax system in as many situations as possible.
The removal this year of the compulsory savings will at one stroke do more to simplify our tax returns and our tax structure than almost any other step I can think of. When we introduced compulsory savings we realized that we would have to make provision for persons who had contractual obligations for savings, and accordingly documents had to be drawn up which would provide for the reporting to employers by employees of the insurance payments they had to make, of the payments on principal on mortgages on their residences, of their payments into pension funds and so forth. The fairer we made it, the harder the forms were to make out and the more complicated they became. With the removal of the compulsory savings entirely, all that vast amount of work by employers and employees, by the taxpayers, and to a certain extent by the employees of the income tax branch disappears. It is a great measure in the extension of simplification.
I want to come now to perhaps the main criticisms of the budget. One suggestion made is that overtime be untaxed, that there be no tax on overtime earnings. The hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) was making the argument the other day that money earned by overtime work should not be taxed. I want to thank the hon. member for the courteous and sympathetic reference to myself which I appreciate greatly, and I really regret that I interrupted him in the course of his speech. I felt that I had to interject and say that the untaxing of overtime earnings would be impracticable and inequitable, and I want to give my reasons for that.
Do not let any one in this house think that an immense amount of consideration has not been given to this proposal. I want to give the reasons why it would be both impracticable and inequitable. In the first place it is contrary to the basic principle of taxing according to ability to pay. Our whole taxation system is based upon the progressive principle that the more a person earns, the higher rate he pays. We do not try to ascertain whether one man works harder than another or works longer hours than another,
whether one man has more ability than another or anything like that. It would be entirely impracticable to try to make inquiries and form judgments on factors of that kind. We must realize that the higher the income, the greater the rate of taxation, and it would be a violation of that principle not to tax the amount earned on overtime.

Economists and critics of the income tax in the thirties and forties and fifties in Great Britain were arguing against this progressive principle of taxation. I do not know whether they said it ignored human nature, but they took very much that position. They said it was not fair to impose a higher rate on a man with higher earnings because he had earned that himself; it was due to him; he had earned it by his own industry or by his own ability or something of the kind, and therefore there should be a flat rate on all earnings. I used to read some of the articles in the British quarterlies on that and I found them very interesting. However, the enlightened opinion of mankind finally came to the conclusion that the progressive principle was the proper one.
If we were to lay down the rule, as the Progressive Conservative amendment suggests, that earnings on overtime were to be untaxed we would have to define overtime; we would have to define normal time. Would normal time be the same in every industry, or would it vary with different industries? I presume it would vary with different industries. In one industry a man would be taxed on what he earned between forty-four and forty-eight hours a week, let us say, and in another industry he would not.
