I do not think it would. Then there is the question of piece workers. How shall we define what is overtime for piece workers? Then there is the question of the returns to be made at the end of the year where a person would have to specify the amount he had earned in overtime and the amount he had earned in normal time. There would be the greatest incentive in the world to overstate overtime earnings and understate normal time earnings. We would have to ask employers to make annual returns breaking down the remuneration paid to employees into normal and overtime. There would be a complexity of accounting in connection with the withholding of tax at the source.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) suggests that it would lead to countless arguments between employers and employees. Would it have the effect of inducing people to work overtime for a few weeks and then stay away from work for a week or two? It may be suggested that I am reflecting upon the workers of Canada, but I have tried not to do that. We have the evidence of a great many members of parliament that taxation has something to do with absenteeism and with the refusal to work overtime. We have.had that evidence not only from members of parliament, not only from employers but from employee organizations. The untaxing of overtime would not solve the ordinary absenteeism problem, which means working less than standard time.
Finally, I cannot find any country where overtime earnings are exempted from taxation. It seems to me that that is an overwhelming case against a very plausible suggestion. Suggestions are put forward by employers here and there who think they could work it in their own industry, but they regard their own

industry as an integer, a unit unrelated to other industries of the country and to the great mass of the Canadian people. The more the thing was considered by the government, and it was very carefully considered, the more apparent it became that it would be impracticable and that it would be inequitable for us to exempt overtime earnings from taxation. That was one of the suggestions of the Progressive Conservative party.

Consequently a farmer, the son of a farmer or a farm helper who was exclusively or principally employed or occupied as a farmer on March 21 of that year would in future be presumed indispensable as such to agriculture, unless there should be contrary evidence. That was the tenor of a conversation I had with
an officer of the army who was the right hand of the deputy minister of national war services. The very same day the same gentleman wired the registrar, giving a shade of difference to the official interpretation that he sent me. This was his wire:
Substantially the interpretation given by Mr. Pouliot is exact. I shall have to make clear the interpretation that I have given to Mr. Pouliot, that the individual concerned shall make a request for postponement to the registrar. as before. And, naturally it is the mobilization board, the national war services board, which will decide whether the applicant is essential to agriculture, according to paragraph 14, subparagraph 3 of the regulations, as modified by order in council P.C. 2252 dated March 21. With the reservation of that supplementary explanation the interpretation given by Mr. Pouliot is correct.
This is signed by the director of mobilization.
Well, sir, it was entirely different. In the first place it was stated that the applicant, the farmer, had the modus vivendi in his favour, which meant that it was up to the board to prove that he was not a farmer and essential on the farm. On the other hand it was left to the board to decide what to do.
Who is the 'lawyer, even the most eminent counsel in the country, who would not be baffled by such a contradictory interpretation? And mind you, sir, when it comes to the interpretation of a statute, the member of parliament is a lawmaker. But when it comes to the interpretation of an order in council it must be the high officials in the department concerned who give the right interpretation. What can anyone do when that interpretation is as contradictory as this one was? It is most difficult.
Then, let us go In between. Other statements have been made by the Prime Minister, one of which is found at page 922 of Hansard for June 19, 1940. It is found at the bottom of the first column and the top of the second. That statement was made by the Prime Minister after I had suggested the raising of a whole battalion in my county for the defence of Canada. I had said that in the caucus room, and I was very much flattered when the Prime Minister reported to the house what I had said in caucus. My name was not mentioned, but since I have referred to the Prime Minister's statement I shall read it. Mark you, sir, I had shown my good will by offering to raise a battalion for the defence of Canada. It was in conformity with the law of the country at the time, when the mobilization act was about to be passed. This was only for the defence of Canada, and I was abiding by the law of the land and showing my good spirit.

The Budget-Mr. Pouliot

Here is what the Prime Minister said:
An hon. member on this side of the house made the statement publicly this morning that he felt he could go into his constituency and, by making it known to his constituents that this measure had to do with the protection of Canada and our own Canadian soil, bring forward in a very short time men from the forests, from the fields and from the factories, all prepared immediately to join the Canadian forces to resist any possible invasion, and that he would be prepared to guarantee that that could be done in constituency after constituency throughout the country, once it was understood that there was the necessity of defending our own Canadian shores. I pointed out to him that in doing tha-t he might be making the greatest mistake possible with respect to the national interest; that, to win this war, we might wish to keep at work in the forests the men who are now working in the forests, to provide .tile timber which will be required for docks and wharves and required immediately; that the men who are working in the factories may be a thousand times more useful to the government of this country in giving their skilled labour to the manufacture of aircraft, munitions or other weapons of war than they could possibly be in lining, up and presenting themselves for military service; equally that on the farms, if we are to perform what will be expected of us, we shall need all the production that can be effectively and rapidly carried out on tbe farms of our country.
I have stood by what the Prime Minister Said on that occasion. At the time there was no plebiscite. That was not said to gain any votes. It was said after an election. It was to be the voluntary policy of the government, and that policy was to keep the farmers on the farms. It was a good policy. And it was just the same for those in essential industry. I withdrew my offer afterwards and, when the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) asked us to indulge in recruiting for overseas I wrote him- and said that since our chief, the Prime Minister, had precluded me from recruiting for the defence of Canada, how could he, as Minister of National Defence, invite me to do recruiting for overseas? I received no answer. Yet Judith Robinson published this in Toronto, and said that it should appear in every paper across Canada.
There are many other things I wish to say. Not only did the great lawyers not understand the contradiction between the statement made in the house by the Prime Minister, and that made outside the house by the Minister of Labour, but even the great brains of the Ottawa Journal used this title in an editorial which was published on Monday, April 6, 1942, "Government Lines Crossed." It reads:
There appears here needless confusion over a fairly important matter; confusion that starts grousing and harmful talk.
Not only lawyers, but even journalists, the brightest of all men, found that it was obscure
[Mr. Pouliot. J
and hard to understand. Not only that, but the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) has lent me a compilation from a return he received, in which were set out the number of boards, commissions, orders and actions. We do not count any more by small numbers; we count by millions. Nearly half a million orders have been issued by clerks, dollar a year men and everybody else. The exact number was 495,488, plus 45,000 orders in council. That is the number of orders issued since the war began. I doubt if there is a room in this building large enough to contain all those publications.
Some of those orders were most important. There is order A-1182 dated April 22, 1944, dealing with rolls of tissue paper. This amended another order and the object was to make the rolls tighter in order to save 'space. I regret having to mention these things, but it shows the scope of the law making by people outside parliament. There is order A-1201 dealing with water-closet seats. They have consolidated three orders in this one. There was the original order; it was amended and then this order amends that one again. There was another one dealing with felt hoods for ladies' hats. Many other things like that are covered. It is childish that orders are passed for such things and published in the official publication. It makes it difficult for those who want to know exactly what is the law.
Let us go a little farther and see what department passed the largest number of orders. Agriculture passed eighty-three; finance, thirty-five; trade and commerce, five; wartime prices and trade board, 1,684, and Department of Labour, 493,681. Nearly all the orders were passed by the Department of Labour which deals with the mobilization of man-power. The Department of National Defence is not mentioned.	.
Would it be possible for the premier of any province to check the 493,681 orders to know if something had happened affecting the mobilization regulations? Nobody could do that. Nobody knows anything about it. I spoke of this to a man well versed in the law and he told me it was due to the war. When I asked him if it would continue after the war was over he said that if it did it would be unbearable. It is a most abnormal situation.
I should like to refer to the way in which the national war services regulations have been amended. We heard a lot about one month, four months and the duration. When the change was made to four months it really meant for the duration, and I will explain why. The first order in council, P.C. 3905 of September 17, 1940, covered the thirty
The Budget-Mr. Poidiot
days training. Then on March 18, 1941, P.C. 1910 was passed for four months, which would expire on July 18, 1941. It was for that period or for such other period as the Minister of National Defence might from time to time prescribe.
On July 2, 1941, an army order signed by the Minister of National Defence was issued which extended the training period for the duration. Those who were in for four months from March could not get out in July because of the order signed by the Minister of National Defence. P.C. 1910 for four months was passed on March 18, 1941, during the season when many farmers were in the forests. It was the dull season and advantage was taken of this fact to extend the period for four months. The farmer had a little leisure and he could take one month's training.
Another great mistake was made in passing the national selective service regulations also in March during the dull season when many farmers were not on the land. The Prime Minister, who has a country place but who is not a farmer, said that the farmers were frozen on the land. I am sure he meant it, but on the other hand a large proportion of them were not there. This created a lot of difficulty which was increased by the press release sent out by the Minister of Labour.
1 regret deeply that there is not a different procedure in the Department of National Defence with reference to those who are badly needed on the farm. Many times I have asked for men who were needed in different places, by their brothers-in-law, by their close relatives, by their uncles and by other people. Although these cases were most meritorious it was impossible to get a satisfactory answer. The Minister of Labour has written to the premier of Quebec stating that farmers will be as well treated as they are everywhere in Canada. There is no exception for Quebec. When I fight for the farmers, as I said yesterday, I do not fight just for the farmers of my constituency or of my province; I fight for the farmers of Canada. What we get for the farmers of our province we get for all the other farmers in the country. There are many farmers who have met their obligations on time.
It was considered a favour to renew a postponement. That is precisely the reason why the chairman of the board in Quebec city was removed and replaced by somebody else. Every time a farmer went to the board and asked for a postponement of his military training the chairman said: "I grant you this favour," and he would grant the man a postponement once, and then a second time, but the third time he refused to grant a further 100-2974
postponement although it was impossible for the farm to be run without the man. To-day I have seen one man who comes from a county far from mine. He is in the army. One of his legs is one and a half inches shorter than the other; he suffers from rheumatism, and he has been put in category A. His father is old and ill; his mother has been ill for eighteen years, and this farmer's son would like to help his father with the cattle on the farm. He is of no use to the army. But all he could get was "no" from his commanding officer. At other times it is still worse because when a man makes his application for postponement he is told by his commanding officer that his application is approved although it is not. It is unfair to treat a man like that, but many a man has suffered injustice just by being treated in that way.
When an application for postponement is made to the commanding officer it is sent to a kind of technical board on which there are men who have no technical experience, especially in farming. Invariably the board decides that the boy is in the army and shall remain there. The board gives its decision in accordance with what the Minister of National Defence said yesterday in his remarks. So long as this thing is not corrected, and so long as the Minister of National Defence does not change his attitude regarding the farmer and does not understand that the farmers are essential to this country, it is unfair for the Minister of Labour to say that we have no conscription for farmers. Every possible means are used to bring the boys into the training camps, and once they are there it is impossible to get them out for any reason, because, as the Minister of Labour has said, the authorities consider that the first duty of a man is to get into the army. If I fight for the farmer, it is not because I am not supporting the army;
I believe that the army should be well fed; that the population of this country should be well fed, and that our allies should receive the surplus after the army and the civilian population of this country have been taken care of.-That is only reasonable.
If hon. members will look at Hansard of February 19, 1943, they will find that I put on the record a list of the members of parliament who have stated that the farmers should be exempted. That was said even by those who speak against the province of Quebec. Were they sincere or were they not? If they were sincere in saying that the farmer should be exempted from military training and that he is following an essential occupation in the war, they have no reason to complain against the province of Quebec. They have no reason to attack the handful of members of parliament who fight for the farmer in this house
The Budget-Mr. Pouliot

as well as for others engaged in other essential industries. They have no reason to attack the premier of Quebec. We are in common in fighting this war, and the farmer deserves to be recognized as being the equal of any other man in this country and, what is more, evidence should be given of that. We are the lawmakers. We should see that all the orders and regulations, even the orders in council, which do not do justice to the farmer should be corrected by legislation passed in the House of Commons, and that no one shall indulge in false pride by not saying a word on behalf of the farmer who is so essential in this war as well as in peace. It is the easiest thing in the world to uproot the farmer; but, mind you, once a farmer is uprooted he is finished with the land. He does not want to. return to the farm. I do not believe in these schemes to bring soldiers on to the land. There may be a few who will make a success of farming, but they will be the exception. I believe that in fighting for the farmer I am fulfilling a national duty.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I want to give a word of special praise to an old friend of mine, Alderman Joseph Matte of the city of Quebec, who wants to investigate the manner in which young draftees have been dealt with in British Columbia. These young men are so far from home that it is hard for them to get home on leave because it takes so long. These young men who abide by the law should be respected by their commanding officer. He should not try to make life impossible for them. Therefore I say that Alderman Matte and the city council of Quebec deserve special praise for their stand in this matter, and I hope they will be .successful in having a probe conducted into the manner in which these young men are treated. I hope also that Alderman Matte will be appointed as a member of the board conducting the inquiry.
All of this has been said, Mr. Speaker, to try to bring the house back to fundamentals, in order that we shall not forget the essentials while we are discussing the most important issues before the country.

Mr. Speaker, on June 23 last when I spoke on the amendment to the budget, I placed on the record certain figures regarding the country of New Zealand. On July 3 the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) in his speech endeavoured to correct some of the figures which I had given on June 23. I am sorry that under the rules of the house which prohibit a member from speaking more than once on the amendment, it has not been until this late date that I have had an opportunity to correct once for all the figures given and the

statements made by the hon. member for Cape Breton South. I am now taking the very first opportunity of placing accurate, authentic and up-to-date figures on the record.
I do so for two reasons. The first is that I have been very careful ever since I came into the house and into public life to be in a position to substantiate statements I make in public, and I am pleased with my record in that respect. Secondly, I do so because of the attitude of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, who for a number of years have gone through the length and breadth of Canada and on every occasion possible have cited conditions in New Zealand, pointing out that if the people of Canada had only a government like the government of New Zealand, a new heaven upon earth would1 open for the people of this country.
I propose this evening to explode that picture, because it is just a picture. I have noted that, whenever I make a statement in the house, immediately it becomes known, particularly in British Columbia, the henchmen of the C.C.F. run into print and, rather than quote entire figures, just say I am mistaken and am making a lot of false statements. I come before the house to-night with statements with which I challenge the factory of scientists which the C.C.F. have, and any hon. member in the house, because I shall quote the actual facts from New Zealand itself, and I have their records before me.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South was rather "cute"-I use the word advisedly -because when he quoted his figures he knew, I think, that I was quoting the latest available statistics, whereas he had gone back to the 1941 records, which gave the figures of 1940, and then endeavoured to compare them with those of 1942. But as every hon. member knows, especially in this time of war great changes occur in each country every year, especially in incomes and expenditures.
Before I have finished I shall-unlike the hon. member-give exact dates with respect to every figure I am going to quote. I shall endeavour to leave no room for complaint other than that hon. members opposite cannot contradict what I am going to say.

When they are going through this country telling the people about the labour government of New Zealand being like the C.C.F. party I wonder if they would mind telling the labour unions and the labour people this story. In New Zealand they have what is known as the flat wage schedule. The artisans, the men of ability who may spend seven or eight years learning a trade in that country get on the average only five cents an hour more than the ordinary helper. I want them to go out through the country and tell our artisans that if we adopt the same kind of government in this country as they have in New Zealand we might have that here. I should like them to tell the people this also. On looking through the records I find that they do not pay the women in comparison to the men anything like what we pay them in Canada, because they pay them less than fifty per cent of what the men receive. I want the public to be told these facts; that is why I am making these remarks to-night. I have had some experience in British Columbia since 1935; if I had time I could tell many queer stories of what happened in that province during the years of depression up through the Fraser valley, but I am not going to deviate from the story I have to tell, because it is too good. I want hon. gentlemen of the C.C.F. to tell the people of Canada the truth, and I am giving them the truth to-night; not the political truth but God's truth.
New Zealand, it is true, is the most protected country in the world, but that does not give its people a particularly high standard of living. We should think that over carefully. I could quote the leader of the opposition - in New Zealand, who says of the labour government that it has left a trail of broken promises. In connection with that great ceremony my mind goes back to the ceremony we had this afternoon when we welcomed that great French soldier, General Charles de Gaulle, in front of the parliament buildings. He is a soldier who has fought the reactionaries of the world since 1934. He finally fought his way to a place of power and recognition by the peoples of the world. I

The Budget

Mr. Gillis
wonder how sincere many of us were this afternoon in that great ceremony. My stand is well known in the circles he moves in. It leaves me a little doubtful at times as to what the future holds for Canada.
The hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) pointed out something this evening that is ancient history. Most members of this group know the fight for social reform that has been carried on for thirty-five or forty years in New Zealand. While many of those reforms were put on the statute books of that country when the old-line parties were in power it was done because of the pressure of the socialist and labour movements. We have a repetition of that history in Canada to-day. We have family allowances and other reform legislation which were promised by the Liberal party as far back as 1919 but which were never enacted. To-day this legislation is before the house. Why? Because they want to give it to the people of Canada? No. It is there because of the pressure of organized labour across Canada in its march in the political field. That has forced a general recognition on the part of the old-line parties that social reform must come. If the people do not get it from the government in power, they will do what they did in New Zealand; they will throw them out.
The figures that I put on the record are still there. If they are wrong, then the Canada Year Book for 1941 and 1942 is wrong. If they are wrong, then the New Zealand Year Book for 1941 is wrong. I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Usley) made it abundantly clear this afternoon that in comparing debt, interest and so forth of different countries there are many ramifications to be considered. There is no exact blueprint and you cannot make any particular statement with respect to debt. You must take many factors into consideration.
When the hon. member for New Westminster put his figures on the record I searched for comparable information. I could- have taken the 1942 figures, but the only information I could find comparable with the figures he put on the record was in the 1941 and 1942 year books which gave the 1940 situation. The 1940 figures with respect to debt, social legislation and so forth are the only figures that can be taken as a comparison with the New Zealand situation.
I could go to-morrow and get the war debt, that has accumulated in Canada since the outbreak of the war and compare it with New Zealand's, because that is what the hon. member did to-night with his figures for 1942. The 1940 figures are the only comparable
figures that should be used in comparing the two countries and those are the ones I used. The hon. member for New Westminster carefully shied clear of what they get for their taxes. To make a general statement about social security does not mean anything.
I have put a clear, concise statement on the record with respect to taxation. I said that no one complains about paying taxes; no one quarrels about any tax imposed by a government if he gets something for it. That is the point. I do not want to go over my figures again and waste the time of the house, but they showed that in the field of social security and education Canada spends only $15.83 per capita while New Zealand spends $39.50.
Anyone who attempts to justify the existing social legislation in this country by comparing the debt and interest charges of Canada and New Zealand has a lot to do. New Zealand is a small country with a million and a half people. It is a barren island with little or no resources, but that country has given its population one of the highest standards of living in the world. It has done that with nothing to work on. We live in a country that covers the north half of the north American continent. We have unlimited resources and 11,500,000 people to provide for. To attempt to justify our situation by .comparing our country with a country like New Zealand is certainly not statesmanship.
Personally I recognize New Zealand's limitations. During the process of fighting this war I am accepting literally the provision of the Atlantic charter for free access to the raw materials of the world. I see Canada in the future helping to raise the standard of living of those countries which have not the wherewithal to provide for their people. I hope that not many hon. members are going to take small countries with few resources as an example in an effort to justify our own inactivity in developing our natural resources. We should not attempt to justify that simply because some other country has not done it. That is the position the hon. member for New Westminster takes to-night.

Those are the things we are fighting for, and those should be the social objectives of each and every country. I am

very sceptical when a member of this house attempts to quarrel with the figures, as has been done on two occasions.
But more than that, I am afraid to-night of the statesmanship of the men who sit on the treasury benches opposite, men who should have the respect of the people of this country and should show more statesmanship than to laugh and applaud when someone occupies the valuable time of this house in trying to ridicule and belittle a sister dominion which is fighting shoulder to shoulder with Canada on every battlefront of the world. I am afraid of that kind of statesmanship. As a member of this House of Commons I take my duties seriously. I am here to see that the people of this country, in every section of it, are protected. I am here to see that our service men get a deal. When we talk of all the things that we have done for our service men, I say that what we have done so far leaves much to be desired. I am going to leave it to the service men to give their answer on that.

The hon. member for Cape Breton South says that the member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid) was belittling New Zealand, whereas the hon. member for New Westminster was actually belittling the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation arguments drawn from the case of New Zealand, and drawn incorrectly, as the hon. member for New Westminster pointed out.
The hon. member for Cape Breton South rose, he said, to defend a sister dominion. No one in this house in my hearing has ever attacked any dominion of the British crown anywhere, least of all the hon. member for New Westminster to-night. He never brought up these figures in the first place-

He did not. The figures were brought up by the C.C.F. on the hustings from one end of Canada to the other; and when figures are brought to meet them, to show how inaccurate they were, the C.C.F. raise objections and say that we are attacking a sister dominion. Who began these comparisons? Mr. Speaker, on two occasions I myself have urged that comparisons between different countries are misleading and should not be made except for the purpose of healthy emulation. But for a year and more past the C.C.F. in Canada have been using facts and figures, they say, derived from the experience of New Zealand, particularly for the purpose of influencing Canadian electors, and now when these alleged facts and figures are met, they say that there is an attack on New Zealand. The attack is on the C.C.F. figures on New Zealand and on their failure to take into account the total picture of New Zealand, which must be taken into account.
The hon. member for New Westminster did not mention to-night the great contribution which New Zealand has made to the war in the way of man-powrer, a contribution which is

The Budget-Mr. Claxton
surpassed by few countries on the face of the earth. He discussed facts and figures in the light of the facts and figures brought up by the C.C.F., and did nothing else. That drew the hon. member for Cape Breton South out of his seat to give a speech which did not add very greatly to our knowledge of this subject. Then the hon. member for Cape Breton South says that our side, when we meet his facts and figures, are producing political propaganda. Let us have more political propaganda if it produces.the facts and gives to the people of Canada the facts upon which they can base their decision in the days and months and years that lie ahead.
When I rose to speak to-night I had not intended to deal with this, but wished to deal with another subject related to it, the need of all the people of Canada getting all the facts about every subject. The prosecution of the war and the preparation for the peace are in the forefront of the minds of all of us, of members of all parties and of all the people of Canada to-day. Whether we are legislators or men working in the factories or on farms or soldiers fighting overseas, all our thoughts and energies and hopes are concentrated on these two objectives. The one essential ingredient for the effective prosecution of the war and for the preparation for the peace is that the people of Canada should remain united in will and in purpose. This has been frequently urged by members in all quarters of the house, but things have been said recently in the house and outside it which do not make for unity.
The unity of any Country depends upon general understanding. We must recognize our common interest in the common good. Any understanding can be based only on knowledge and truth. The effective working of a democracy depends upon the knowledge of all the people and in their interest in their own government. This is particularly so in Canada, with five geographical divisions, a country where most of the people are descended from the two races which have given to the western world its major civilizations. Judged by any standards, Canada has done well through the years of peace and through the years of war. Even if we look backwards it is hard to say where our total effort on behalf of the united nations could have been increased.
Moreover, the measures adopted by this government have led to the burden of the war being fairly distributed on the shoulders of the population in relation to their ability to bear the load. When one considers the differences which we must recognize do exist in Canada and the difficulties that have been overcome, the record of the people of Canada
stands up better than the record of the critics of Canada. The great majority of Canadians are anxious to remain united in the war and in the peace. The great majority of Canadians are prepared to face facts realistically and to make their utmost effort to get along together in the recognition that along any other road lies disastef. The great majority of Canadians deplore the attempt by anyone which has the effect of diminishing unity or dividing the country into separate races and creeds. Unfortunately there are in all parts of the country groups that respond to sectional and racial appeals, and there are unfortunately people who make those appeals.

The hon. member bases his assertion in Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere on the facts that "Rasminski, Petegorski and Kentchum have been appointed to posts of command." Let us take "Kentchum" first. Undoubtedly, by "Kentchum" he intends to mention David Ketchum, who is an officer of the wartime information board. The family have been on this continent for some hundreds of years, and as far as their records go back their origin is completely Anglo-Saxon or Irish.
Let me come to Messrs. Rasminski and Petegorski. Both these men were born in Canada and they are of the Jewish faith. Mr. Rasminski was educated at the university of Toronto and the London school of economics. For many years he was on the economic staff of the League of Nations. He is now an assistant to the governor of the Bank of Canada. He is known in Canada and throughout the world as one of the outstanding banking economists of the whole world. If the people of Ste. Anne de la Pocatiere could meet Mr. Rasminski they would find a gentleman who could speak French, who would delight them and charm them with his knowledge of and love for their country, and who would impress them with the great services which he has given to oiu- country.
Mr. Petegorski is an employee of the national film board on loan to the wartime information board, where he had to do with

his own special field of labour relations. He is a graduate of Columbia university, and after taking a post-graduate course at the London school of economics he became a professor at Antioch. He is a born Canadian, and he has, like any other born Canadian, the right to serve Canada.
These two men and a handful of others who are of the Jewish faith are in the service of the government of Canada. Are they to be deprived of the responsibility of serving Canada because they are of a faith different from yours or mine? Is Canada to be deprived of the advantage of having their services? Are we to limit ourselves to people of Anglo-Saxon descent, or French descent or some other descent? The duty of serving Canada must not be limited to people of any one race, and the right to serve Canada is not limited to people of any race. It should be the glory of Canada that this is one place on earth where myths of racial superiority and racial prejudices shall not flourish.
We ought to recognize the facts. We are a country of minorities. Every race in Canada, whether English or Scottish or Irish or French or Ukrainian or Jewish or German or anything else, is a minority with reference to the whole; they are in a minority when viewed in the total picture of the people of Canada. Every person in Canada, with the exception of the Indians and Eskimos, is descended from immigrants. We ought to be proud of that fact, and proud of what our forefathers did for us in settling in this country and pioneering for us. Hitler advertised race theories and the world has seen what they mean. In fact his reign of terror is best expressed and understood by the violent anti-Semitism which has been, not his article of faith, but his stock in trade. When we join in anti-Semitism of any kind, when we join in giving voice to racial theories of one kind or another, we point Hitler's sword at our own breasts.
Since the hon. member who mentioned this is of the Catholic faith, may I recall to him- and I do it with the utmost respect-the word of his Holiness Pope Pius XI, who had this to say:
Abraham is called our patriarch, our ancestor. Anti-Semitism is not compatible with the sublime reality of this text. It is a movement in which we Christians cannot share.
Spiritually the people who give way to racial prejudice, who breed intolerance by their own intolerance, who create injustice by being less than just, are walking in the footsteps not of Christ but of all that Christianity and humanity stand and fight against in this war. The province of Quebec, my own native province, to which I am deeply attached, having

The Budyet-Mr. Claxton
been bom there and descended from people who lived there for three generations, is not to-day predominantly rural. It is no longer self-contained. Seventy per cent of the people of that province are urban. No part of industrial Canada is so dependent for its livelihood and prosperity on trade outside Quebec, with other Canadians and with the people of other countries. Quebec's interests are not isolationist, but above all places in Canada and, indeed, almost in the world, the interest of Quebec lies in the greatest possible cooperation with the people of other provinces and of other countries.
To-day we have been honoured by the presence of General de Gaulle. He paid his tribute to the sons of French parents who in the Canadian regiments were among the first to land on the beaches of Normandy from which their ancestors had come just three hundred years ago. For most of them it was their first return to the home of their ancestors. They went overseas to bring freedom to France and to humanity. Let us not lose that freedom at home. Freedom is a very civilized thing, and so is tolerance. Civilization is measured by the degree of freedom and the amount of tolerance there is in any community. We can be free economically and socially only if we have the advantages which come from united action and agreement on common objectives. And on those objectives we are not so far apart as the hon. member for Cape Breton South would like us and the Canadian people to believe. We can be free and united only if we have that respect for the individual which is the hallmark of Christianity. We can be united, provided that we keep before us the concept of Canada as a country second to none on the face of the earth.
A few days ago a friend of mine received from his son overseas a letter in which this was said:
It is a funny thing, I never really felt as proud of being a Canadian until I got down here with some of the best fighting men in the world and -found what respect they hold us in. Our chaps made quite a name for themselves in the last war and in this one they are living up to that name and doing one better. The more I see of people and countries I thank God I am a Canadian.
The Canada that boy is thinking of is the rivers and lakes, the open spaces and the dark woods, the mines and factories, the farms and the city streets. It is the history of Canada that it has roots in two civilizations that have led the western world; and it is in the geography of Canada with its back to the pole and its arjns stretching out to the two oceans, bound to Britain by no ties except -ties of interest and of affection, associated with the
United States in a friendly relationship, the depth and the extent of which other nations cannot even understand. When he speaks of himself as a Canadian this soldier overseas is not thinking of an English Canadian or a French Canadian or a Jewish Canadian, he is thinking of a Canadian, an unhyphenated Canadian, and so are his comrades in arms, and so are the vast majority of the people of Canada to-day. They want to keep away from all the isms, from all the hyphens and to be people living in this great country of ours, people not only with a past that anyone can be proud of, but people with a future better than that of any other country. That is the kind of Canada he is thinking of, and that is the kind of Canada we in -this house mean to give him.
The truth is that we can accomplish almost anything in Canada if we stay united. The war has shown that. But what advantage would it be to the people of Quebec or elsewhere -if the seeds of disunity are planted, flourish, grow up and separate race from race, creed from creed, province from province? Unity is not a lofty ideal; it is a stem neces- -sity if our welfare is to be served.
Mr. Speaker, I -referred by name to the gentlemen I did because of the speech of my hon. friend to which I have referred. I hold no particular brief for those of the Jewish faith or of any other faith. I say- that people who come to Canada and settle here have the right [DOT]to be treated as all other Canadians, that there should be no discrimination between people in Canada whether they be of one province or another, of one race or another, or of one faith or another. It is our job in this house to see that as far as it lies within our power everyone in Canada is given equal opportunity to give our country what he can give it and to make for himself, his family- and his descendants a life in this country such as only this country can give if we stay united.
But in any country having interests as wide as Canada's, national unity- can be founded only on a cause which is larger than the nation itself. Patriotism begins at home, but it must not stop there in this world of little distances. The unity we seek must extend beyond the national borders. The unity we seek is essential to prosperity at home. The unity we seek must include the larger unity beyond our borders, which is also essential to our prosperity. We have everything before -us if we stand united. We have nothing but weariness, difficulty and dissension if we allow these racial discords to be encouraged in our midst.
I feel that I make what may seem a rather prosaic statement in this house at this time, but I feel it deeply and I feel that I am voic-
The Budget-Mr. Dorian

ing the views of those men whom I have met in our armed forces and of those people in Canada whom I have met, who say that they want to see this Canada grow strong as Canada, as a country stretching from sea to sea, as a country which we can be proud to work for, to die for and to live for.

speechtext:
On matters on which all the hon. members who have the least bit of common sense had to vote with us.
Mr. Speaker, it is most unfortunate that such happenings should occur among hon. members from my native province. We, citizens of French extraction, who, no later than this afternoon, were so proud to hear the voice of France through General de Gaulle; we who,

The Budget-Mr. Dupuis
in 1763 transferred our allegiance from France to Britain, and who, thanks to the spirit of justice which is predominant in all British citizens have obtained freedom of action in this country; we who, in spite of this freedom, have to fight those who oppress, through their might and their money, the weak and the working classes; we who form a minority in this country, who should always remain united, should ever work hand in hand when the interests of the province of Quebec are at stake, wThat have we seen in this house, especially during the last few years? We have witnessed, in the province of Quebec, the very same unfortunate events that occurred at the Bourbon palace in the years before 1939, when Frenchmen, instead of remaining united and preparing to fight Hitler, the modem tyrant, were divided and fighting among themselves.
Despite the inspiring example given by our former motherland, we, the citizens of the province of Quebec, give the same evidence of disunion, we give the sad example of that dissension which the great Mercier stigmatized in days gone by when he advised his fellow-citizens from the province of Quebec to put an end to their internecine strife and achieve union among themselves.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay is one of those people, I do not blame him personally for that, I rather ascribe it to an old habit and to a mediate cause arising from the intellectual training we get in the province of Quebec, to the individualism from which we suffer so much rather than to a personal and intentional shortcoming on the part of the hon. member.
He is neither a conservative, because he has disowned the conservative party, nor a liberal, for he has never been one, nor again a member of the Bloc populaire, because I think that group does not want him, nor a supporter of the C.C.F., because that would not do in Charlevoix-Saguenay since the C.C.F. is but a camouflaged communism and the Charlevoix-Saguenay people value their money too much to hand it out to parasites. He belongs to no party. He is his own party.
Next to him there is the Bloc Populaire party, whose members for reasons and motives I shall not mention, because in their conscience they know them all too well, have left the Liberal party to wend their way toward a region as dismal and cold as a block of ice, in an attempt to bring down to their own level a man whose shoe-laces they are not fit to tie, the honourable and distinguished leader of the Canadian government. I shall not call him the greatest statesman, because that expression has become too commonplace,
nor will I call him a great diplomat because too many people are labelled so, but I shall designate him as one of the liberators of mankind. Because of his contribution to the freedom of the working classes, some people have endeavoured to vilify him, to sully his reputation by resorting to all kinds of arguments with a view to bringing about his downfall in the province of Quebec. This has gone on to such an extent that people like the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay and young green-. horns who support the Bloc Populaire, when Ihey want to ruin the good name of the Hon. Mr. Godbout in the eyes of his fellow-citizens, accuse him of working hand in hand with the Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King, as if that were unworthy and scandalous, as if it were a humiliation to enjoy the friendship of the hon. the' Prime Minister of this country.
Mr. Speaker, far from being humiliating or shameful, for one to proclaim himself the friend of the Prime Minister of this country, I maintain that it is a great honour, because he has contributed to the supreme greatness of this country. Let the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay listen to this carefully: I say that it is providential, in these tragic times, when the world is plunged into the most terrible of all wars, a prey to the greatest scourge which mankind has ever known, I say it is providential that the government of this country should be led by a man as gifted, experienced, patriotic, broad-minded as the present Prime Minister. I challenge the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay to try to reach even to his shoe-soles.
The future Prime Minister of Canada, after extensive studies in economics, furthered his training in thought and meditation, in appropriate surroundings under the guidance of his mother, the daughter of a great patriot who joined us in 1837 in the fight for freedom.
In 1908, through the grandfather of the present postmaster general (Mr. Mulock), Sir William Mulock, he was appointed in Ottawa by the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier -to the position of editor of the Labour Gazette. Why did he take this responsible post? Because that young man had found that the labour classes-workers and farmers-did not receive justice in this country, or at least they did not receive the full measure of justice to which they were entitled. He gave such a good account of himself that the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier set up a department of labour with William Lyon Mackenzie King as minister. Since then, he has seized every opportunity to protect the interests of the working class, to fight abuses committed by capitalists.
The Budget-Mr. Dupuis

I would point out, however, Mr. Speaker, that I am not denouncing all capitalists, for there are honest capitalists. I am in favour of freedom of production, of private enterprise, and in this democratic country of ours I am in favour of allowing all young men to prosper and to develop the talents with which Providence has endowed them.
But, there are capitalists who overstep the mark and who may be compared to those who committed similar abuses in 1837 and against whom we rebelled.
That young man, destined later to become Prime Minister, devoted his life to devise and submit to the parliament of this country laws to protect the working classes, the workers, the farmers, and to prevent the trusts from making an abusive use of their capital. He had laws enacted against these capitalists, against the trusts, and he saw to it that they were complied with. For twenty-five years, he proposed laws in favour of workers, giving them the right to organize and to protect themselves against those who were not acting fairly. We shall celebrate, on the seventh of next month, the twenty-fifth anniversary of his nomination as leader of the Liberal party. And when our friends of the Bloc, or the so-called independent members or the other parties in this house suggest social legislation, they should remember once for all that they are merely following, and from a distance at that, the path blazed by the Right Hon. the Prime Minister of this country.
Mr. Speaker, it is true that if there is in the province of Quebec an insignificant minority of citizens who are against our participation in this war, who are against everything we do, who seize upon every opportunity to say that we are fighting for England, that we do not owe anything to England, that the English are not doing anything, that young Englishmen hide in this country, that we are defending England, I should like to take this opportunity to inform the house 1 and the citizens of my country, of the attitude of well-thinking citizens of Quebec and of those of the other sections of the country whose origin is the same as mine. Every human being in this world is actuated by a principle of primary importance, which is the ultimate object in life. It is the pursuit of happiness. While it is never reached, through our work, our energy, the virtues which we acquire through the principles which were instilled into our minds by our parents and by the clergy of any of the Christian denominations to which we may belong, we may hope on such solid basis to follow the path which was assigned to us by Providence.

The main factors in the achievement of such an ideal include the love of freedom, freedom of speech, freedom of action, freedom of expression, freedom for our Christian clergy to teach, freedom to own property, freedom for us all to use as we choose the reward of our labour or the income derived from whatever property we may own. Those are the great freedoms which to us mean more than anything else in the world. Since the last war, which had no character of finality, our traditional enemies prepared in stealth and through all the crafty means they could design to destroy that freedom. But, on our part, we merely relied in the first place upon the League of Nations because we always advocated peace, and secondly, in case of war, upon the Maginot line built in France, which in that country was held to be impregnable. That explains why the right hon. the Prime Minister of this country, the hon. the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power)-to whom my hon. friend from Charlevoix-Saguenay has referred-the former minister of public works, the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres (Mr. Cardin), the late Right Hon. Ernest Lapointe, whose memory we cherish, and all the government's spokesmen said, before the downfall of France: We shall wage a moderate war, Canada will send only a token army overseas. However, in June, 1940, after Czechoslovakia had been crushed and Austria invaded; after Poland had been attacked; after England and the other united nations had declared war; after all these events had occurred and France, our former mother country, with Belgium, had fallen and the French government, having taken flight to the south of their country, had been forced to ask for an armistice, where is the reasonable man who, considering the special events of these unfortunate times, would not have modified his views. The hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay and the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Choquette), who honour me by listening to my remarks at this moment, had the greatest confidence in the Maginot line; however, when we saw it breached and when we witnessed the fall of France, would it not have *been sheer foolishness if, for the simple reason of stating with pride that our opinions had not changed, we had refused to alter our views with regard to our participation in the present war?
As General de Gaulle said this afternoon, in view of the easy flow of transportation, and thanks to modem inventions, the countries are all bound together; absolute sovereignty has ceased to exist in the world; all nations must help one another, and, in the present armed conflict not a single democracy was justified

The Budget-Mr. Picard
in remaining neutral. As for us Canadians of French ancestry, after our former mother country was crushed by the foe, we knew that Canada would have the same fate unless England resisted to the end; we knew perfectly that the freedoms we have enjoyed since the conquest would have been lost forever if we had not realized that our sacred duty was to take our share of this war and to help Britain who was struggling alone when all the European countries were under the nazi yoke.
Mr. Speaker, has my time expired? If the hon. members of this house will give me a few minutes more, I shall be through.

Mr. Speaker, as a member of French descent, I feel it my duty, despite the lateness of the hour, in view of the speech of the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Dorion) to make a few remarks. I had intended to speak on the budget, but had given way to others in order to shorten the debate, because we thought it might be over by the end of last week. I do not wish now to make the speech which I had intended to deliver. However, I feel I must rise to state emphatically to this house that the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay does not represent the views of Quebec but the views of a boisterous minority. To my mind no French Canadian does more to harm his people than one who stirs up prejudice for political purposes.
French Canadians have had long and strenuous fights to gain recognition of their rights, but, 185 years after Canada became British, seventy-seven years after confederation, it can be said that no rights are denied to our people. The fight is no more for rights; they are not denied, except by a few bigots who have no influence even with their own people. The fight is now for obtaining some of the privileges which derive from those rights. The fight may be to obtain more in the way of public appointments. I wish to point out to our friends of English descent that more harm is done to national unity by not recognizing this, and because in some
of the government services they do not give us our share, ammunition is furnished daily to ultra-nationalists and isolationists and others in Quebec who stir up prejudice. Were we treated more fairly in some quarters these people would be deprived of an argument which they bring up on the public platform in Quebec. If we did not have in some of the government services in Montreal people who do not know a word of French, although they deal daily with French people, and have to get an interpreter to sit by them when they have in front of them a Quebec farmer; if we did not have in the city of Quebec employed by the wartime prices and trade board a man who, although his French is confined to the equivalent of "yes" and "no" and a few other words, is retained under the pretext that he was formerly with a packing company-per-sonallj'-, probably, a nice chap, but one who can barely understand the people who speak to him-while such small incidents continue, although they are small they are aggravating. Every day our people meet these men and are incensed about it, and that sort of thing gives material to the ultra-nationalists to stir up prejudice.
Yet I say that it is not by raising racial prejudice that these people will help our race. It is by understanding, by discussing questions dispassionately, as in this house, with the best of faith and the best of intention to cooperate, that we can attain results. I repeat that it is by mutual understanding that these results will be achieved, not by going on the platform, as the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay has done in the present election, and trying to raise racial prejudice.
When hon. members hear such statements as have been made by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay and are occasionally heard in the Quebec house from some other members, they may have a small idea of the difficulty experienced by those of us who are trying, in order to bring unity and harmony in this country, to interpret English Canada to French Canada and French Canada to English Canada. On the one side we are faced with the intolerance of certain of the public servants who do not want to give us what is our share; on the other side we are faced with the intolerance of bigots of our own people who try to excite others against the English majority, and are now about to enter upon a campaign of anti-Semitism. Day by day some of these people, instead of granting to others the tolerance they ask for themselves, get up on the platform and make such statements as those which were made at Ste. Anne by the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay. Nothing can be more harmful. I repeat, and I should
The Budget-Mr. Picard

like some of the "patriots" of my own race to understand it, that there is nothing more harmful than statements of that kind. When they are taken to task, as has been done so aptly to-night by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton), they do not deny it, but they hide behind a smokescreen and enter upon a tirade on political lines. That is what we have to face, those of us who understand that the country is larger than the limits of Quebec, that our country is Canada, extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific, that we as Canadians have a great role to play.
What are we faced with when we go .to Quebec? We meet the kind of propaganda, the counterpart of which is also found in other provinces and of which oftentimes we have evidence in this house in certain quarters when statements prejudicial to our people are made, and on a vastly larger scale, outside this house. If Canada is to enter again the era of intolerance, what of our future? I appeal to those who are trying to work for national unity. There are some such, I would say, in each of the political parties in this house, for I would not wish to monopolize for my own party all claim to goodness.in that respect. However, I believe that as far as Quebec and French Canada generally is concerned it has received more comprehension, more understanding and vastly fairer treatment from the present administration than it has from the friends of the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay, the people whom he supported and whom he tried to elect in 1940.
Before resuming my seat

and I have promised that I will not speak at length-I wish to state emphatically that the statements of the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay made at Ste. Anne, the statements he has repeated to-night, and others of the same type which are spread daily in Quebec, are not the views of the majority of the province. They are nevertheless a very dangerous current of opinion, and I appeal at the same time to my friends of other groups to try to understand our people. Those of us who are endeavouring to act as a go-between try to get the people of both sides to understand one another and to make compromises. Here again I repeat that never has the province of Quebec or the French Canadian minority in this country experienced fairer treatment than by the present administration, not in the way of favouritism, but in the way of fairness and equity.
The attitude of mind which we find in certain people on platforms in Quebec, that attitude of intolerance which is to be found in some people in other parts of the country, would not have the influence it has were it not for the press of the English language which, whenever a member in Quebec makes a foolish or rash statement, prints in big broad lines, "French Canadian says this"; but 'when, the next day, somebody makes a constructive speech, he will get two lines on the last page, if he gets that much. The same thing is true so far as our French nationalist press in Quebec is concerned. When a crackpot of some sort like Shields gets up and makes a crazy statement it is put all over the province. I admit that the fault is on both sides. I appeal to both sides now while there is yet time, not to carry on with the id on of prejudice and intolerance, but to work together in a spirit of harmony for the greatness of Canada.
Mr. S. II. KNOWLES (Winnipeg North Centre): Mr. Speaker, had I caught your eye an hour ago I might have spoken for twenty minutes in this debate. However, I appreciate the desire of the government to conclude this debate to-night if at all possible; therefore I shall take only a few minutes in the hope that the debate can be brought to a close.
First of all I should like to offer my congratulations to the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Claxton) and others who have associated themselves with him in his fervent plea for racial tolerance and understanding in this country. There is such a thing as a liberal democratic tradition. That liberal, of course, has a small "L". Those who share in that tradition are, as the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard) has just said, not confined to any one party. The fact is that on all sides of this house there are members who value deeply the ideals and the concept of humanity as stated to-night by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, as well as by some of the other hon. members who have spoken. I felt encouraged when the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George was speaking in connection with another point that is in the minds of some of us. I refer to the fact that in due course I hope we are to have an opportunity to do something about the miscarriage of this principle which occurred in connection with bill 135 some time ago; and I am glad to feel from what has been said to-night by a Liberal member that there are in that party a great many who share his view and who in the liberal democratic tradition will join with some of the others of us in what we hope will happen when that bill comes before us.

The Budget-Mr. Knowles
However, with an eye on the clock and remembering my promise, what I should have liked to have time to do would be to make a contribution-I feel it would be that-to the debate that we had earlier this evening on the question of New Zealand. Had I the time I would have given the house the information contained in material that I have in my hand which was prepared not by the government of New Zealand or any opposition group trying to discredit that country, but rather by the International Labour Office at Montreal. This material sets out in factual form the actual social benefits that accrue to the people of that dominion. To give even the headings of this material that I have would take more time than there is left at my disposal. But on some future occasion perhaps that opportunity will be presented, and I should like to give that material when that opportunity comes.
The point I wish to make has in fact been made by some of the others already, namely, that you get nowhere in this kind of argument when you attempt to compare tax rates and national debt and all that kind of thing. As the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) pointed out this afternoon, national debt has to be set against the ability of the country to carry it; it has to be set against the standard of employment and standard of living generally. Also, when you look at tax rates you have to find out what proportion of the total taxes collected by the country, not just the taxes of one kind, but what proportion of the total taxes are levied according to ability to pay; but even after you have done all that in the most complete statistical form it is still just about impossible to array two systems against each other in that way. I feel, however, that there is merit in looking at the things that the people of New Zealand actually have in the way of complete social security benefits, and on another occasion I shall, because I think hon. members should have it, place a digest of it on Hansard.
There is one other reference that I shall call to the attention of hon. members. This time it is a book from New Zealand entitled " New Zealand, the Working Democracy," by Walter Nash. I refer hon. members in particular to
appendix 3 of this book on pages 318 and 319, in which there is set out in tabulated form the benefits that were paidl to New Zealand people under the social security laws in effect when the labour government came into power in 1935 and the benefits in effect in 1943. This table answers one of the arguments made to-night.
Hon. members have already made many comments about our having so much to say about New Zealand. We have no apology to make for that. As a matter of fact we feel we have done the people of this country a service in printing by the thousands such a speech as that which was made in Ottawa in 1941 before the committee on reconstruction and rehabilitation of this house by Walter Nash, a speech in which he set out the things that they were doing in that country. I myself had something to do with that reprinting in Manitoba and I know the orders that kept coming in amazed us. They showed the interest of the people in what was going on down there. We feel that we are doing a service to the people of this country in pointing out what has been done in that sister dominion. As a matter of fact I am reminded of the words of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid), who spoke in this present debate on June 30 as reported at page 4386 of Hansard. He said:
As one who was born in the same country, indeed in the same neighbourhood, may I pay my humble tribute to one of Scotland's sons who has made a name for himself by his public service to New Zealand and thereby to mankind.
I feel that in line with what the hon. member said on that occasion, rather than what he said to-night, we are doing a service to the people of Canada in making known to them as widely as we can the service that has been rendered to their people by the labour government of New Zealand.	.
Main motion (Mr. Ilsley) agreed to on division.

speechtext:
Your Excellency, Your Royal Highness, ladies and gentlemen: We are met this morning to extend to General Charles de Gaulle a hearty welcome to Canada.
To you, General de Gaulle, as a French soldier, as a leader in the fight for world freedom, and as representing the unconquerable spirit of France, I am proud to offer this welcome in the name of the government and people of Canada.
Here, in the presence of the representative of the crown, are assembled before you the representatives in parliament of the Canadian people. Here also are assembled residents of our capital city. All are proud to honour the man who in the darkest days of this war rallied the forces of Free France, and who to-day is the symbol of the determination of the French nation to restore its freedom and greatness.
In welcoming General de Gaulle to our country, I can speak for the whole of Canada. In no country has the sympathy for France in her agony been deeper than in our own; in none have the prayers for her liberation been more fervent; in none has the growth of French resistance been watched with greater pride and admiration.
For the visit to Canada of General de Gaulle, the hour could not have been more happily chosen. At this moment, French and Canadian soldiers are fighting side by side in Italy. On the battle fields of Normandy, Canadian fighting men form part of the great allied striking force. Amidst these scenes of conflict and triumph there has been a proud renewal of the historic association between the people of France and Canada.
General de Gaulle comes to us fresh from his visit to Normandy. What emotion he must have felt as he set foot once more on the soil

of France! What a thrill of pride was felt in many Canadain homes when we learned that the first troops he met in Normandy were men of Canada's army! It was from Normandy that the first Canadians came to make a new home and found a new nation in the new world. We rejoice that Canada's fighting -men are helping to-day to free the ancestral home of so many of our people.
France is not only the ancestral home of many Canadians; in France are many shrines sacred to all Canadians. The Somme, Arras, Cambrai, Vimy, and a host of scenes of battle a generation ago, are names that will live forever in our history. In fighting for the liberation of France, Canada is fighting for what is truly a part of herself.
Within France a living spirit of resistance has revealed itself in countless acts of heroism and sacrifice. Behind the enemy's lines the French resistance has been undermining German power. Since the landings in Normandy, underground forces have been quick to strike. On all sides there is evidence that in the hearts of the French people there still burns an unquenchable fire of "liberty, equality and fraternity" which no dishonourable betrayal within, or fiendish tortures from without, have been able to extinguish.
In the revival of French military power, inside and outside France, General de Gaulle's role has been of incomparable importance.
In these years of war, we in Canada have sought to do our part to keep alive the flame of French civiliation. We have continued to cherish our admiration for France and all she has meant to freedom. WTe have never lost our faith that the greatness of France would be restored. The people of Canada are proud to have their part in the memorable events in which the liberation of France is being accomplished.

In thanking you for your visit and in wishing you all that is best in your valorous leadership, I ask you, General de Gaulle, to take back with you an assurance from the Canadian people to the people of France. Tell them that all Canada is united in support of the determination of the allied nations to drive the enemy from the soil of France. Tell them we are not less united in the determination to destroy the power of Germany to terrorize Europe, and to end, once and for all, Germany's capacity to disturb the peace of the world. Tell them that we are with them heart and soul in these days of suffering and1 sacrifice; and tell them to fight on, for we are confident the day is drawing near when we shall be sharing with them their joys and triumphs in the supreme hour of victory.

General CHARLES de GAULLE (Translation) :	The moving welcome that you have
accorded me seems to come from a double inspiration. No doubt you wish first of all to testify to the comforting solidarity which unites in the world across frontiers, oceans and continents, the men who fight together for liberty.
No doubt you have also judged it well to show here that France has not been, is not and never will be forgotten.
Well, gentlemen, I wish to say that for France, Canada is a dearer friend than ever.
Certainly the past accounts for a great part of this mutual sympathy. On the one hand your people, who have never been opposed to ours in any historical event; your people, whose men have always opened their minds and their hearts to the ideas and sentiments which have elevated the French spirit your people, in the veins of many of whom flows blood which has come from France, and on the other hand my country which remembers having been the first to carry Christian and European civilization to this immense land, my country which has never ceased to follow and admire the magnificent efforts of your ancestors and of your kinsmen in their struggle to bring about prosperity through the development of the natural resources of the country and to develop the minds of the people intellectually, spiritually and morally in order to create a state of full consciousness of its own valour and in loyalty to the Commonwealth of which it is a part. Your people and my country- may powerful bonds link them throughout time.
Nothing seemed more natural to old France than to see Canadian soldiers struggling on her soil for the same cause in the preceding world war and to bury reverently in her soil those whose heroic memory is symbolized by Yimy.
And let me say here that nothing has seemed more moving to the man who has the honour to speak to you than to have seen the Canadian Corps engaged on the banks of the Liri River in Italy recently side by side with the French army and to find first upon the beaches of Normandy, where they took a foothold at the beginning of the great battle, a fine and brave Canadian regiment.
(Text):
But, ladies and gentlemen, if the past holds so many special reasons why France and Canada should understand one another, I may say confidently that the present has added a great many more! It is in a time of crisis
fMr. St. Laurent.]
that friendship proves itself. Well, during these difficult years France has passed through many trying days. Submerged by the enemy, stunned by the disaster, betrayed or deceived by those who, having seized the state, did not use either their power or their reputation except to plunge it and maintain it in the shame of debasement, France might for a short time have presented to malevolent or superficial observers the appearance of one of those falls from which a nation does not rise when she has accepted it. But others, better informed because they were more favourable, quickly realized that my country, in the depths of its misery, refused to give up. These understood very soon that the determination, the hope, the spirit of the French people remained firmly at the side of those who refused to lower the flag and who at all costs intended to maintain their country in the camp of liberty.
I will not try to describe what such an enterprise has cost in effort, losses, often bitter disappointments, for the French who in every domain, whether it be in the interior of France or outside the country, have carried on this fierce struggle for independence and for national unity.
But it is my duty to say what comfort and support they have found in Canada, in its government and in its people. The French aviators whom you have trained here; the French forces whom you have helped to arm; the French prisoners whom you have fed and clothed; above all, perhaps, the innumerable French who, in their suffering and their fight, heard the echo of Canadian sympathy, are a witness to this fact.
To-day France is standing upright and united. If the living friendship which she has found everywhere in Canada has contributed to sustain and lift my country during her trials and thus has materially and morally strengthened the coalition of Free Peoples against their bitter enemies, to-day it becomes a very important factor in the task of reorganizing the world which will come out of this terrible war. At present, victory flushes the horizon. We feel in the hearts of the peoples who have united to assure the triumph of right and liberty, a tremendous aspiration towards a better future. For, if so many men and women in a free world have voluntarily suffered, fought, worked, if so many good and brave soldiers have died without a murmur, if so many towns and villages have offered themselves up in sacrifice for our common salvation, it would not be tolerable, it would not even be possible, that from so much death, sacrifice and ruin a greater and better humanity would not emerge.

Privilege-Mr. Lacombe
But, in a world where all intercourse has unceasingly tightened the interdependence of nations at the same time as that of individuals, how is it possible to conceive human progress if not within a system of real international cooperation? For the same reasons that a single war common to all covers the whole of our earth which has become so small, the peace which we will have to make must be a single peace, common to all. For the same reasons that what is being thought, produced, manufactured anywhere in the world has inevitable consequences upon the destiny of the most obscure combatant, thus to-morrow, the condition of man in the world, whatever his race, country or activity, will depend in some measure upon what will be achieved anywhere in the political, economic, social, spiritual, intellectual and moral spheres. In other words, it is impossible to imagine either assured security or solid and lasting progress for any nation or any individual if all nations among themselves, or within each nation, all citizens among themselves, are not willing to consent to work together in normal brotherhood.
France, emerging step by step from her temporary misfortunes, France enlightened by her suffering, France intending no longer to divide, but to unite her passion for progress and traditional wisdom, states herself ready to play her full part in this universal task. She is certain to find, at her side and in agreement with her, all the peoples who know her well- and first among them she will find Canada.
Wednesday, July 12, 1944
